title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?
body_text: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? ../ Preamble A work of art A peek inside Inside the script What does it actually do? Who's behind this? What's next Special Thanks ../ Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? Wed Oct 28 2026 authored by veritas Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js . A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg } Huh? function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation. I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts. Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research. Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request. I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked. Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied! with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
body_text: CircuitHub - Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Capabilities PCB Stackups Design Rules Certifications ProtoBoard Case Studies Careers FAQ Blog Podcast About Us Careers Press Contact Sign In Sign Up support@circuithub.com +1 617-401-0319 Sign In Sign Up Menu G Blog All News Updates Tips Community Back to Site Back to the site Case study Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen News Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Andrew on October 26, 2026 For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand. The problem Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked. Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it. Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops. What The Grid is The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it. Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid. What it means for a real board To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address. Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median. So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165. It's not a prototype The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers. What's next Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027. The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can. If you want to help rebuild the Western electronics supply chain, we're hiring . And if you have a board to build, get an instant quote . title: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
body_text: DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work | Surge AI DAYJOB: Tax A benchmark for AI tax agents Blog benchmarks Off-the-Shelf Training experts Products Enterprise Research Careers Contact Login Menu Close THE SURGE AI BLOG DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work October 27, 2026 October 27, 2026 No items found. TL;DR Real-world tax work is messy. Instructions are incomplete, records conflict, and the most important problems aren't always the ones explicitly assigned. DAYJOB: Tax evaluates whether AI agents can handle that reality, taking ownership of a tax professional's work from an initial client request to a finished deliverable. Across 50 environments and 1,789 files, agents must navigate complex tax records, uncover issues clients may not know to raise, and make consequential judgments with incomplete information. Success requires more than tax knowledge and accurate calculations. It demands the initiative and professional judgment to figure out what needs to be done, investigate what matters, and deliver work that meets professional standards. ‍ LEADERBOARD HUGGING FACE Table of contents Case Study Llama Analysis of Individual writings Appendix Anna was planning to sell her condo. She had moved out in August 2024 and wanted to know whether closing in October 2026 or January 2027 would be better for taxes. An AI agent reviewed both options and correctly concluded that either date would satisfy the residence requirement for a tax break worth up to $250,000 in excluded gains. But it left out an important deadline. Under the usual rules, homeowners must have lived in a property for at least two of the five years before selling it to qualify for the exclusion. Because Anna moved out in August 2024, she would stop satisfying that requirement around the end of August 2027. If her sale was delayed beyond August 2027, she could lose eligibility. Across five attempts, Astra never identified the deadline. Opus identified it in all five attempts. The agent evaluated the proposed dates correctly, but its advice left Anna unaware of a deadline that could affect a major financial decision. A tax adviser should recognize consequential issues even when the client doesn't know to ask about them. This is the kind of professional judgment we're testing with DAYJOB: Tax , the latest addition to Surge AI's DAYJOB benchmark family . Introducing DAYJOB: Tax DAYJOB evaluates AI agents on professional tax assignments requiring specialized expertise, complex materials, and decisions that aren't fully specified in the initial instructions. Our earlier releases covered Healthcare and Finance. DAYJOB: Tax extends that work into tax preparation, compliance, and advisory services. The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice. Agents receive client requests and supporting records, then produce tax returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or client advice. These assignments test professional judgment alongside tax knowledge, calculations, retrieval, and instruction following. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and carry those decisions into their final work. Results: Leaderboard and Pareto Frontiers Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads with a 10.8% pass rate on the DAYJOB: Tax leaderboard , followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%. We report pass@1 at a 95% rubric threshold. An attempt passes when it satisfies at least 95% of the task's criteria, which assess calculations, supporting evidence, consequential issues, and the completed deliverable. Performance versus cost We also compared model performance against average cost per trial. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 occupy the high-performance end of the measured Pareto frontier. The breadth of professional tax work DAYJOB: Tax covers eight areas, each requiring different rules, records, and expertise: Individual and family tax Small-business tax Partnerships Property and investments Estates, gifts, and trusts International tax Corporate transactions Tax review and disputes Some assignments require complete filing packages with supporting workpapers. Others ask agents to investigate transactions, review previous filings, or prepare advice about decisions clients haven't yet made. What's inside the assignments? The benchmark contains 1,789 workspace files , with a median of 30 per assignment and as many as 123. These include 1,487 PDFs, 117 Excel workbooks, 38 Word documents, and additional emails, images, CSVs, JSON records, and text files. The workspaces include filed and draft tax returns, K-1s, W-2s, IRS notices, general ledgers, payroll records, contracts, and correspondence. They also contain the less standardized evidence that tax professionals routinely work with. One assignment includes a photograph of a handwritten receipt for merchandise purchased for resale . The agent must read the item descriptions and amounts, reconcile them with spending records, and determine how the purchases affect inventory and cost of goods sold. Another assignment involves an industrial silo-services company whose client assumes it operates only in Alabama. But its field dispatch log shows crews working across five states . The job locations, crew sizes, and days on site provide evidence relevant to the company's multistate tax obligations. Other environments are similarly varied. One involves a cross-border household whose Polish employment and property records must be reconciled with cryptocurrency exchange exports, wallet histories, and historical purchase lots. Created and reviewed by tax experts DAYJOB tasks begin with real-world professional workflows. Tax experts turn these situations into realistic assignments, developing the supporting records, expected outcomes, and grading criteria. Each task undergoes a three-layer expert review for correctness, completeness, and solvability. Tax experts bring experience across corporate taxation, partnerships, individual returns, trusts, and multistate compliance. Their backgrounds include: Corporate and private-equity taxation: A tax attorney with over 10 years of experience at PwC, Deloitte, and Exxon, covering tax planning, compliance, audits, and controversy. Partnership and corporate taxation: A Baker Tilly Tax Director with experience at PwC, Moss Adams, and Windes, specializing in complex partnership allocations, consolidated corporate returns, REITs, and high-net-worth clients. Real estate and individual taxation: A tax professional with experience at Deloitte and EY, specializing in real-estate partnerships, individual taxation, and trusts. A retirement plan built on an unverified assumption A separating couple asked an AI agent how to divide their Roth IRA and 401(k). Opus 5.5 told them they weren't legally married and recommended keeping their accounts separate, with a cash payment to even out the balances. It opened one response: You aren't legally married, so neither account can be split without triggering taxes and penalties. But the couple's own records raised doubts about that conclusion. Although they now lived in Florida, where new common-law marriages generally aren't recognized, they had previously lived together in Texas and held a ceremony in Colorado. Texas recognizes informal marriages under certain conditions, and a valid marriage established elsewhere may remain valid in Florida. That distinction could change the tax consequences of dividing their retirement accounts. Across all five attempts, Opus based its recommendations around the assumption that the couple was unmarried , even when it acknowledged uncertainty. Astra recognized the need to verify their marital status in four of five attempts. One response advised: We first need to confirm your legal marital status. The client asked how to divide the accounts. The agent needed to establish whether they were married before recommending a course of action. The evidence that should have prompted that investigation was already in the files. Where DAYJOB: Tax fits Most existing tax benchmarks begin with a defined problem: a legal question to answer, a return to calculate, or missing taxpayer information to collect. These evaluations measure important capabilities, but much of a tax professional's work involves figuring out what the problem actually is. Clients provide incomplete instructions, records contain conflicting evidence, and consequential issues may never appear in the original request. DAYJOB tests whether agents can handle that end-to-end responsibility , including identifying issues the client overlooked, evaluating conflicting evidence, and deciding what needs to be done in the first place. TaxBench Can the model answer a difficult tax question? TaxBench evaluates 114 tax questions across multiple specialties, each with a defined problem and grading rubric. DAYJOB also asks whether the client asked the right question. Anna wants to compare two dates for selling her condo. Both satisfy the residence requirement for a tax exclusion, but does the agent warn her when that eligibility could expire? TaxCalcBench Can the model calculate an accurate return? TaxCalcBench evaluates tax-return accuracy against expected filing values, using realistic tax documents and taxpayer scenarios. DAYJOB also asks whether the underlying records actually support the tax treatment. A studio's ledger references an attached receipt, but the receipt is missing. Does the agent flag the missing evidence or incorrectly treat the reimbursement as verified? TaxLab Can the agent gather missing information and file correctly? TaxLab tests whether agents can question a simulated taxpayer, obtain missing information, and complete a federal individual tax return. DAYJOB extends that responsibility across the wider tax profession. The deliverable might be a partnership loss analysis, an estate return, a review of a disputed tax position, or a strategy letter. The central distinction is how much responsibility remains with the agent. DAYJOB evaluates whether agents can discover consequential issues, exercise professional judgment, and carry their findings through to a completed filing, review, or recommendation. What DAYJOB: Tax measures DAYJOB tests whether AI agents can take ownership of a professional assignment from start to finish. That means navigating messy records, identifying issues the client never raised, making sound judgments with incomplete information, and delivering work that meets professional standards. The results show how difficult that remains for frontier models. Even when agents can perform the individual steps, exercising professional judgment and reliably carrying out real-world tax workflows remain out of reach. Agents haven’t yet passed the audit. The full leaderboard, with every model we evaluated, is on the DAYJOB: Tax benchmark page . To learn more or request access to the full benchmark, contact benchmarks@surgehq.ai . title: CNC Stone Carving
body_text: CNC Stone Carving - Carmelite Gothic Carmelite Monks of Wyoming Gothic Gothic Why Gothic Architecture? Gothic Theory Methods for Constructing Gothic Architecture Gothic Elements CNC Stone Carving Stone Setting Resources for Gothic Architecture Our Design Ancient Carmelite Architecture Carmelite Gothic Monastery Gothic Church Design Chapter House Refectory Building Hermitage Porter’s Lodge Progress The Monks Carmelite Monks of Wyoming Gothic Gothic Why Gothic Architecture? Gothic Theory Methods for Constructing Gothic Architecture Gothic Elements CNC Stone Carving Stone Setting Resources for Gothic Architecture Our Design Ancient Carmelite Architecture Carmelite Gothic Monastery Gothic Church Design Chapter House Refectory Building Hermitage Porter’s Lodge Progress The Monks CNC Stone Carving Home » CNC Stone Carving CNC Stone Carving In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place. However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head. (The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.) CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.  The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God. CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk What is a CNC machine CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention. Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process. CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings! CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks Prussiani CNC machines The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs. The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later. The Carving Process The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like.  The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come. Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone.  The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster. The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.   Latest Posts Chapter House First Look Carving a Gothic Finial Coming Soon! title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
body_text: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates ← Main Page Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates 28th October 2026 Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates. Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again. Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago. Why does this matter? Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make. For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted. To check whether your git is affected, run: git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with. To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates. git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED . A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves. You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example: git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run: curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ A certificate error means curl is protected. What should Apple do? Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework. Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem . What can developers do in the meantime? The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix. Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk. Site published by Dennis Jackson . This site is the work of many contributors from the community. The source is on GitHub and PRs are welcome. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 .

title: Emacs Turns 50
body_text: EMACS turns 50 | MIT Technology Review You need to enable JavaScript to view this site. Skip to Content Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue MIT Alumni News: 1865 EMACS turns 50 How the MIT AI Lab’s text editor gave birth to the free software movement. By Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05 archive page October 20, 2026 Artwork from Richard Stallman’s 1981 EMACS manual. Later iterations of the manual featured cover art of a medieval knight riding a yak. The complex yet playful illustrations captured the hacker culture of the era. Internet Archive Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards. A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code. By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display. One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system. EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code. In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time. “Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74 Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT AI Lab, saw a full-screen editor—called E—on a visit to Stanford’s AI Lab. Inspired, he returned to MIT and set out to improve Control-R. The most important change to the program’s underlying structure: Every key ran its own macro when pressed, making Control-R far easier to customize. The lab’s hackers took to Stallman’s code with gusto and started changing and adding commands. That created an issue for Guy Steele Jr., SM ’77, PhD ’80. A graduate student in the lab, Steele frequently needed to help other lab members debug their programs. “I noticed that it was much harder for me to help someone who was using one of these packages rather than straight TECO,” he recalls. “Eventually, it occurred to me to try [to] broker consensus on a standard set of Control-R commands that everyone could agree to use.” David Moon ’75, another member of the lab, helped out. Stallman jumped in as well, and eventually he took over. Together, the group assigned a standard set of commands that made use of the Meta key found on many of the lab’s early keyboards: Meta-F would move the cursor forward a word, Meta-B would move it back a word, and so on. They called the result EMACS, short for “Editor Macros” or “Editing Macros.” “My goal was not to construct a great new text editor,” says Steele. “I was trying to address a social problem.” Nevertheless, EMACS was a great new text editor. Whereas Control-R could be tricky, EMACS users with “no technical experience at all” could learn to edit letters, emails, and even programs “within minutes or an hour,” according to a history by Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74. Meanwhile, “experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Stallman started distributing EMACS to anyone who sent him a magnetic tape and a postage-paid return envelope. “EMACS does not cost anything; instead, you are joining the EMACS software-sharing commune,” he wrote in the 1981 manual. “The conditions of membership are that you must send back any improvements you make to EMACS.” Programming manuals for the Multics operating system. While working at Honeywell, Bernard S. Greenberg wrote his own version of EMACS for the system. It was so good, Honeywell commercialized it. MIT MUSEUM Greenberg, meanwhile, decided to write his own version for Multics, an early operating system by that time owned by his employer, Honeywell. Greenberg’s EMACS won first prize at the International Honeywell Software Conference in 1980, and Honeywell started selling it. Honeywell wasn’t alone in marketing a version of EMACS: James Arthur Gosling, a Carnegie Mellon graduate who went on to lead the development of the Java programming language, made a version that he eventually sold as a commercial product. This transition from free to paid software ultimately spurred Stallman to launch a project to create an operating system that could be freely shared and improved by its users. He modeled this effort, called the GNU Project, after the increasingly popular Unix operating system from Bell Labs. “GNU” was short for “GNU’s Not Unix,” alluding to the fact that, unlike Unix, it would be free. The project’s first major application was GNU Emacs (now restyled in lowercase). The GNU/Linux operating system was still years away, so, despite the project’s aim to create an entirely free operating system, GNU Emacs initally ran on Unix. It would eventually run on a range of operating systems, including Linux but also other Unix-based systems. When Apple launched Mac OS X, the first release of its Unix-based operating system, in 2001, GNU Emacs was included. Apple stopped shipping GNU Emacs in 2019, but the company still has a program called mg (“Micro GNU Emacs”). Though it supports most EMACS commands, it lacks an integrated programming language, making it what some call an “ersatz EMACS.” Meanwhile, much of Apple’s OS still has hidden support for EMACS commands. The keyboard has no Meta key, but Control-Option-B will move back one word, and Control-Option-F will move one forward. by Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05 Share Share story on linkedin Share story on facebook Share story on email MIT Alumni News Made by MIT This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. body_text: 1.4.0 - Release Notes Search docs Ctrl K Esc Docs Discord GitHub Download Download Discord GitHub Ghostty Docs About Ghostty Install Configuration Linux Features Terminal API (VT) Help Financial Support Ghostty Docs About Ghostty Install Binaries and Packages Build from Source Packaging Ghostty Prerelease Builds Release Notes Overview 1.4.0 1.3.1 1.3.0 1.2.3 1.2.2 1.2.1 1.2.0 1.1.3 1.1.2 1.1.1 1.1.0 1.0.1 Configuration Linux Features Terminal API (VT) Help Financial Support Ghostty Docs Install Release Notes 1.4.0 Ghostty 1.4.0 Release notes for Ghostty 1.4.0, released on October 27, 2026. Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release that includes large performance and memory improvements, a 100% complete Kitty graphics implementation including animation and relative placements (the first non-Kitty terminal to do so), SSH integration improvements, and hundreds more improvements and fixes across all platforms. This release features 7 months of work with changes from 172 contributors over 2,889 commits . Thank you to all the contributors, maintainers, community moderators, translators, packagers, and users who each helped make this release possible. These release notes are painstakingly and lovingly hand-crafted by human Ghostty maintainers, including the full changelog. They take a combined 16+ hours to write, so please enjoy. 🥰 Ghostty is non-profit! Please support development. Almost all donations go directly to paying contributors. Learn more about how you can help. Learn more → Security GHSA-4hwh-wx3w-3fqg . Paste protection didn't treat carriage returns as line endings, so a paste could run a command without confirmation in programs that don't use bracketed paste. This requires user interaction (copy-paste) to trigger. GHSA-mhff-mv4q-fp63 . Malicious Kitty graphics commands could crash or hang Ghostty, force huge allocations, or in limited cases read or delete files outside the allowed temporary directories. This only requires displaying malicious output. GHSA-hcr9-7hcr-mjm8 . Malicious terminal output could crash Ghostty, closing every window, via tmux control mode. tmux doesn't need to be installed. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-hp9c-qp4q-cpw3 . The same impact as above, via a tmux control mode layout with a zero-sized or oversized pane. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-w9q4-5jvv-mcv4 . Clearing the screen into scrollback could corrupt memory if it deleted the scrollback page holding a styled or hyperlinked cursor. This only requires displaying malicious output, but only with a small scrollback-limit such as 0 . The default isn't known to be affected. GHSA-2r63-vmw6-3m3c . A crafted directory name could make the zsh shell integration send arbitrary escape sequences, such as silently replacing the clipboard via OSC 52. bash was affected in a more limited way. This only requires cd -ing into a directory from untrusted content, such as a cloned repository. macOS: GHSA-cw69-wm67-5pv8 . Cmd-clicking a crafted OSC 8 hyperlink could open unsafe local files or custom URL schemes, leading to arbitrary command execution. Ghostty now blocks unsafe targets and confirms custom URL schemes. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mfw9-xcr3-7gfp . The same issue as above for links detected by the link configuration, including the default URL matcher. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-v8cw-fg4j-jcc4 . Drag-and-drop text skipped paste protection, with the same impact as above. This requires user interaction (drag-and-drop) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mxqx-236q-wrv7 . Opening a file whose name contains control characters could run a different command than the one shown in the confirmation dialog. This requires a crafted file on your system and confirming the dialog. Note: I requested CVEs for the above advisories weeks ago, but GitHub hasn't assigned them yet. If/when they're assigned, I will update the above with proper CVE numbers. Highlights macOS 27 Support PRs: #12999 #13069 #13393 #14413 #14414 Ghostty 1.4 supports macOS 27 (Golden Gate). Most of the work was compatibility fixes: Tabs in the titlebar ( macos-titlebar-style = tabs ) lay out correctly again. The native tab bar no longer draws as a solid gray bar on top of your theme. It now lets the new glass style blend with your terminal background. macos-titlebar-style = hidden no longer covers the top lines of the terminal when Reduce Transparency is on. The app icon no longer has a thin border. The Shortcuts "New Window" action no longer opens two windows when Ghostty is running without any windows. Ghostty 1.4 remains fully compatible with prior macOS versions back to and including macOS 13 (Ventura). See the system requirements for more details. Note Ghostty 1.3.1 works on macOS 27, but it has some of the visual issues listed above, such as the gray tab bar. Kitty Graphics Animation and Relative Placements PRs: #13943 #13939 #13935 #13934 #13893 #13933 #13389 #13270 #13281 Ghostty now supports Kitty graphics animation and relative placements . These were the last major features of the Kitty graphics protocol that Ghostty didn't support. Programs that display animated images with the Kitty protocol, such as an animated GIF shown with kitten icat , now animate in Ghostty instead of showing a single still frame. Frame transmission, composition, and playback control are all supported, and animations pause while the terminal isn't visible. Relative placements let a program position one image relative to another image's placement, so the child image moves along with its parent. We also did a full conformance pass against the specification and Kitty itself, fixing dozens of behavioral differences. For example, images now scroll with text inside scroll regions ( #4323 ), retransmitting an image ID replaces the old image ( #6711 ), and invalid image data now gets an error response instead of silence, which could leave clients hanging. The full list is in the terminal capabilities section. Kitty graphics are faster, too. Image payloads are now parsed in bulk with SIMD instead of one byte at a time, making large image transfers about 16x faster to parse in our benchmarks (64 MiB of image data, x86_64 Linux), and drawing images costs much less per frame. Our Kitty graphics implementation now covers 100% of the published specification, making Ghostty (and libghostty) the first terminal to do this outside of Kitty itself. Scrollback Compression and Lower Memory Usage PRs: #13264 #13473 #13240 #13245 #14130 #14137 #14138 #14017 Ghostty now transparently compresses scrollback that isn't visible, reducing the physical memory those pages use by 70% to 90% for typical text-heavy history. Compression only runs while the terminal is idle and pages are decompressed on demand when you scroll back or search, so it has no measurable impact on I/O throughput. Thanks to compression, the default scrollback limit has been raised from 10 MB to 50 MB per terminal. On platforms that support compression, a full scrollback still generally uses less physical memory than the old 10 MB limit did. Note Compression lowers resident (physical) memory, not virtual memory, so look at resident memory when measuring it. It is currently available on macOS and 64-bit Linux. Beyond scrollback, memory usage is lower in many places: A new, empty terminal now uses about 16 KiB of terminal page memory on macOS, down from 128 KiB in Ghostty 1.3.1. On macOS and Linux, memory freed by clearing or trimming scrollback is now returned to the OS instead of being held until the terminal closes. Hidden tabs release their GPU resources. On macOS, with one visible tab and 20 hidden tabs, GPU memory dropped from about 385 MiB to 18 MiB. Rebuilding them when a tab becomes visible again takes under a millisecond. Performance Improvements PRs: #13209 #13220 #13226 #13227 #13537 #13827 #13587 #14011 #13722 #14035 #12760 There are performance improvements across the board in Ghostty 1.4 that yield significant gains compared to prior Ghostty versions. The biggest win came from a surprising discovery: on macOS, the kernel caps every read from a pty at about 1 KiB no matter how large the read buffer is. Previously, Ghostty processed each read as it arrived, so per-read overhead was paid every kilobyte, and the program writing output sat blocked while we parsed. Ghostty now drains the pty on one thread while parsing on another, raising end-to-end I/O throughput by 25% to 55% on macOS (M4 Max, plain and Unicode text) over Ghostty 1.3.x. VT processing itself is also much faster. In parser benchmarks, plain ASCII text went from 128 MB/s to 725 MB/s (5.7x), CJK text got 3.4x faster, and a 2.6 GB dataset of real-world terminal recordings from asciinema is processed about 25% faster. Together, these changes took cat -ing a 150 MB text file on macOS from 1.5 seconds to 566 milliseconds. Other notable improvements: Resize: resizing a terminal with a large scrollback is about 6x faster (120x80 with 10,000 lines of scrollback), and 3x to 5x faster with history full of CJK text or emoji. Rendering: the renderer holds the terminal lock 2.7x to 11x less per frame, leaving more time for the I/O thread during heavy output. Copy and search: formatting terminal contents as plain text, HTML, or VT, which backs clipboard copy, write_screen_file , and scrollback search, is 1.5x to 8x faster. Launch (macOS): about 15% faster from launch to visible window, and 27% faster to the first rendered frame. Idle energy: on macOS, the renderer's display link now sleeps when there's nothing to draw. On GTK, hidden tabs stop rendering, matching macOS. Large OSC sequences: OSC 52 clipboard payloads parse about 30x faster , and even short sequences like title changes are about 6x faster. New OpenGL Renderer (Linux, FreeBSD) PRs: #14052 #14269 The GTK app has a new rendering pipeline. It no longer uses GtkGLArea . Instead, the renderer draws with EGL on its own thread, exports each frame as a DMABUF, and hands it to GTK to display. Rendering is now triple-buffered, which should greatly reduce tearing, and no OpenGL calls run on the main thread anymore, which let us remove a number of workarounds. The most visible result is crisp text under fractional scaling. Text and box-drawing characters are no longer blurry with fractional display scaling such as 125% or 150% ( #1938 ). We fixed this once before, but it came back after upstream GTK changes. Ghostty now renders at the window's true fractional scale, so every rendered pixel maps to exactly one pixel on screen. The new render surface needs a system EGL library (see Changes for Package Maintainers ). On GPU drivers that can't export DMABUFs, Ghostty falls back to copying frames through the CPU, which is slower but works. Kitty Clipboard Protocol PRs: #13962 #13993 #13995 #13998 #14002 #14061 Ghostty now implements the Kitty clipboard protocol (OSC 5522) on both macOS and GTK. Ghostty 1.3 could parse the protocol but didn't implement it. OSC 52 can only read and write plain text. The Kitty clipboard protocol lets programs running in the terminal read and write any kind of clipboard data, such as images or HTML, and lets them pick among the formats on the clipboard. Programs can also enable paste events (mode 5522), which tell the program what formats a paste contains so it can read the one it wants. This is how a terminal program can accept a pasted image, for example. Clipboard access follows the existing clipboard-read and clipboard-write configurations. By default, reads prompt for permission and writes are allowed. The permission prompt shows a preview of the clipboard contents, including images. Programs that send a password can have your answer remembered for the rest of that terminal session. A new clipboard-write-limit-bytes configuration limits the size of a single write (default 64 MiB). A write over the limit fails and leaves the clipboard untouched. Split Drag and Drop (GTK) PRs: #10423 #13706 You can now rearrange splits on GTK by dragging them, matching the macOS feature introduced in Ghostty 1.3. When a tab has two or more splits, each split shows a drag handle at the top. Grab the handle and drop the split onto any other split, including splits in other tabs and windows. An overlay shows which side of the target split it will land on. The terminal contents, working directory, and running processes all move with it. A new drag-handle configuration controls when drag handles are shown on both macOS and GTK: auto (default), always , or never . With never , splits can't be rearranged with the mouse. Hiding the handles was a common request from users who found them in the way. On GTK, splits can only be dropped onto other splits. Dragging a split out to create a new tab or window is macOS-only. Terminal Emulation Accuracy PRs: #14454 #13494 #14483 #14538 #14673 #14375 #14144 Ghostty 1.4 includes dozens of improvements to core terminal emulation. We now run esctest , Thomas Dickey's terminal conformance suite, against Ghostty's terminal core in CI. Alongside that, we fixed many differences from xterm in cursor movement within margins, tab stops, character sets, mode reports, and more. You can find the full list of related changes in the terminal capabilities section. Ghostty also supports several new sequences, including soft terminal reset (DECSTR), extended cursor position reports (DECXCPR), backarrow key mode (DECBKM), and screen size reports in characters ( CSI 19 t ). Programs can also now ask whether the terminal is visible using visibility reports (mode 2033), so they can stop rendering while hidden. Keyboard encoding also matches xterm more closely, with fixes for modifyOtherKeys mode 2 and legacy Alt-as-Escape encoding of non-ASCII keys. Two new sequences are disabled by default because they can be abused by untrusted programs, including ones running on a remote machine: # Allow programs to resize the window (CSI 8 t) vt-window-resize-allowed = true # Allow programs to request screen checksums (DECRQCRA) vt-xt-checksum-report = true SSH Integration with ghostty +ssh PRs: #12582 #12814 #13533 #13844 #14472 #14854 Ghostty 1.2 introduced SSH shell integration features as a work in progress. In Ghostty 1.4, they're backed by a new ghostty +ssh CLI action: a drop-in ssh wrapper that prepares the remote session for Ghostty and then runs the real ssh with your arguments forwarded unchanged. ghostty +ssh user@example.com # Or alias it so every ssh invocation goes through it alias ssh= 'ghostty +ssh --' Before connecting, +ssh installs Ghostty's terminfo on the remote host so the proper xterm-ghostty TERM value can be used, and forwards COLORTERM , TERM_PROGRAM , and TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION . If the terminfo install fails (for example, tic isn't available on the remote), it falls back to TERM=xterm-256color . Flags such as --terminfo=false , --forward-env=false , and --verbose control each step. The ssh-env and ssh-terminfo shell integration features (still opt-in) now call +ssh too. Previously, each shell integration carried its own copy of this logic, which made up roughly a third of our shell integration scripts. Now bash, zsh, fish, elvish, and Nushell all behave identically, and you can get the same behavior from scripts or anywhere else by calling ghostty +ssh directly. The terminfo install itself is also more reliable. Ghostty now always installs its own bundled terminfo rather than accepting whatever xterm-ghostty entry the remote already has, and it reinstalls automatically when a Ghostty update changes the terminfo. It also no longer needs infocmp or Ghostty's terminfo on the local machine. Installs are cached per host and port, so two machines behind one address no longer share a cache entry. And ssh-env no longer silently overrides SetEnv entries in your ~/.ssh/config ( #11518 ). The +ssh-cache command that manages this cache now takes positional destinations ( ghostty +ssh-cache user@example.com ) and has a new --prune=30d flag. See the breaking changes if you script against +ssh-cache . System Requirements macOS: The minimum required macOS version for Ghostty 1.4 remains unchanged (macOS 13 Ventura). Ghostty is now compatible with macOS 27. GTK: Ghostty 1.4 requires GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7 , up from GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 in Ghostty 1.3. This aligns with our GTK/Adwaita version policy . Notably, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS doesn't meet this requirement. Systems with older GTK or Adwaita versions can work around this requirement by using an older version of Ghostty or the Flatpak package. #14330 OpenGL (GTK): The minimum required OpenGL version remains 4.3, but Ghostty now renders through EGL instead of GTK's OpenGL widget. This should be invisible for nearly everyone, but if Ghostty fails to start with an EGL error, please make sure your GPU driver provides a working EGL implementation. Important We previously announced that Ghostty 1.4 would require macOS 14. Nothing forced our hand to do this in this release, so we kept macOS 13 support. We still plan to drop macOS 13 in a future release. Apple dropped security support for macOS 13 in the fall of 2025, so we recommend upgrading regardless. Breaking Changes The following behaviors have changed in 1.4.0: copy-on-select has been reworked and now accepts none , primary , clipboard , or both . The meaning of clipboard has changed: it previously copied to both the selection clipboard and the system clipboard, and now copies only to the system clipboard. If you set copy-on-select = clipboard and want the old behavior, change it to both . #12600 #12604 macOS: copy-on-select now defaults to none (previously true ), so selecting text no longer copies it anywhere and middle-click paste of the selection no longer works by default. To restore the 1.3 behavior, set copy-on-select = primary . Note that an explicit copy-on-select = true on macOS now copies selections to the system clipboard, which is different from 1.3. #12600 #12604 macOS: cmd+arrow_up and cmd+arrow_down now run jump_to_prompt again, matching Terminal.app and Ghostty 1.2. In 1.3, these keys were hardcoded to scroll to the top and bottom and couldn't be rebound. To keep the 1.3 behavior, set keybind = cmd+arrow_up=scroll_to_top and keybind = cmd+arrow_down=scroll_to_bottom . #12245 GTK: The default ctrl+shift+page_up and ctrl+shift+page_down keybinds now move the current tab left and right ( move_tab ), matching Firefox, GNOME Terminal, and VS Code. jump_to_prompt moved to ctrl+shift+arrow_up and ctrl+shift+arrow_down , so programs running in the terminal no longer receive those keys. If a program you use needs them, unbind them with keybind = ctrl+shift+arrow_up=unbind and keybind = ctrl+shift+arrow_down=unbind . #4998 #12458 Deprecations The list below contains deprecations that remain compatible today through a compatibility layer, but may break in a future release if they are ignored: scrollback-limit has been renamed to scrollback-limit-bytes , to make room for the new scrollback-limit-lines . #13473 copy-on-select = true is replaced with copy-on-select = primary on Linux and FreeBSD, or copy-on-select = clipboard on macOS. copy-on-select = false is replaced with copy-on-select = none . #12600 #12604 There is no set timeline to remove these deprecations, but we recommend adapting to the new configurations sooner rather than later to avoid any possible disruptions in the future.
