(SS2/SS3) now apply only to the next printed character. #14576 vt: Tab clear (TBC) fixes: CSI 0 g no longer sets a tab stop where there wasn't one, and CSI g with no parameter clears the tab stop at the cursor. #13900 #14644 vt: Printing with autowrap (DECAWM) disabled clears the pending wrap, so re-enabling autowrap doesn't cause a spurious line wrap. #14652 vt: With reverse wrap enabled, moving left after restoring a cursor with a pending wrap no longer jumps the cursor. #14390 vt: Cursor movement respects margins and origin mode: CUB and backspace stop at the left margin, and CHA, HPA, VPA, HPR, and VPR no longer apply the margin offset twice in origin mode. #14761 #14762 vt: Fix a crash when VS15 narrows a wide character under the cursor. #13631 vt: Fix a crash or memory corruption after narrowing the terminal cuts a wide character in half on the alternate screen or with wraparound disabled. #14509 vt: Fix a crash when a grapheme cluster widens in the last column and wraps inside or below a scroll region with grapheme clustering (mode 2027) enabled. #14552 vt: Fix a slow memory and performance leak in graphics-heavy sessions where evicted Kitty images left their placements' tracked positions behind. #13656 vt: Fix a memory leak when an OSC color sequence contains more than two requests. #13239 Shell Integration A new ghostty +ssh CLI action wraps ssh and sets up Ghostty on remote hosts: it forwards Ghostty's environment and installs Ghostty's terminfo on the first connection to each host, caching successful installs. It can be used directly ( ghostty +ssh user@example.com ) or as an alias ( alias ssh='ghostty +ssh --' ) without shell integration. The ssh-env and ssh-terminfo shell integration features now use it for every shell. #12582 ssh-terminfo now always installs Ghostty's bundled terminfo on remote hosts instead of keeping an existing, possibly outdated, xterm-ghostty entry, and reinstalls it when a newer Ghostty changes its terminfo. #13844 ghostty +ssh-cache has been reworked with positional destinations, a new --prune option, consistent output and exit codes, and error messages that name the cache file. See the breaking changes above. #12814 #13533 ssh-terminfo now tells apart the same host on different ports, so terminfo is installed on each of them. ghostty +ssh-cache accepts host:port destinations. #14472 ssh-env no longer overrides SetEnv entries in your ~/.ssh/config . #11518 #14854 bash: Failed commands now report their real exit status on Bash 4.4+, so command finished notifications no longer report every command as successful. #14247 #14250 nu: Tab completion for ssh and sudo now works with external completers such as carapace. #13310 bash: The bundled bash-preexec, used only for Bash versions older than 4.4 such as macOS's /bin/bash , has been updated to 0.7.0. #14120 zsh: Fix a stray { in the prompt and broken prompt marking when PS1 or PS2 ends with a bare % . #11832 bash: Fix "command not found" errors in subshells that inherit PROMPT_COMMAND . #11690 bash: Fix a syntax error when an existing PROMPT_COMMAND ends with a newline. #11621 bash: Fix extra blank lines at the prompt when using ble.sh. #11644 bash: Fix the shell integration hook being added twice when it is sourced again with an array PROMPT_COMMAND . #14266 macOS macOS: Support macOS 27. This fixes the layout and background color of titlebar tabs, a thin border around the app icon, hidden titlebars covering the top lines of the terminal with Reduce Transparency enabled, and the Shortcuts "New Window" action opening two windows. #13001 #13390 #14107 #14411 #12999 #13069 macOS: When a terminal's process exits, a native bar now appears at the bottom of the terminal instead of text being written into the terminal. Commands that fail or exit faster than abnormal-command-exit-runtime are highlighted in red. #7649 #12251 macOS: Quitting, or closing a window, when multiple windows or tabs have running processes now offers "Review Windows...", which steps through each one so you can decide what to close. #12742 #14062 macOS: The command palette now highlights matching text, matches initials, searches action descriptions, and ranks results by where they matched. #12264 #13610 #13624 macOS: The search bar now remembers the last search and shares it with other apps through the system find pasteboard, like Safari and Terminal.app. #12516 #12712 macOS: Screen readers such as VoiceOver are now notified when the selection changes instead of reading a stale selection. #12902 macOS: The AppleScript terminal class and the Shortcuts terminal entity now expose pid (of the foreground process) and tty . #11592 #10756 #11922 macOS: AppleScript tabs and terminals have a new read-write name override property to set or clear a custom title. #12048 #14733 macOS: Middle-clicking a tab closes it with macos-titlebar-style = tabs . #11962 #11963 macOS: The version in the About window now links to the release notes for that version. #11964 macOS: Updates that are downloaded and installed automatically no longer prompt you to restart. Checking for updates manually still offers to restart. #13623 macOS: toggle_background_opacity now applies to every tab in the window, and new windows inherit the current state. #11583 macOS: cmd+arrow_up and cmd+arrow_down now run their configured keybinds, which default to jump_to_prompt . Ghostty 1.3 always scrolled to the top or bottom of the scrollback instead, ignoring the configuration. To scroll to the top or bottom, use cmd+home and cmd+end . #12245 macOS: In the configuration errors window, Return reloads the configuration and Escape ignores the errors. #12601 macOS: Ghostty launches about 15% faster to a visible window and draws its first frame about 27% sooner. #13722 macOS: Terminals that aren't visible, such as background tabs, now release their GPU resources and rebuild them when shown again. With 20 background tabs, GPU memory drops from about 385 MiB to 18 MiB. Metal buffers also no longer over-allocate when they grow. #14017 #13490 macOS: Lower idle CPU and energy use. The display link now pauses when there is nothing to draw, and unfocused terminals that are animating draw at most once per display refresh instead of once per write. #14035 #14068 macOS: Update Sparkle to 2.9.6, which fixes several security advisories in Sparkle, including CVE-2026-47121 and CVE-2026-47122. #14072 #14082 macOS: Global keybinds no longer stop working after macOS disables Ghostty's event tap. #12294 #12714 macOS: Fix IME composition issues. Korean text being composed is now committed instead of lost when pressing an arrow key, and control-key IME shortcuts such as Japanese input's ctrl+j no longer send control characters to the terminal. #11461 #12447 #12518 #12547 macOS: Text from input methods, dictation, and the emoji picker is now sent as typed input instead of pasted text. Programs no longer treat dictation as a paste, and switching input sources mid-composition sends the pending text as keys, matching Terminal.app. #13195 #13222 #13817 macOS: Unicode Hex Input can now enter characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as emoji, typed as surrogate pairs. #13733 #13737 macOS: font-thicken now also applies to IME preedit text. #14230 macOS: option+backspace and other modified Backspace keys now report their modifiers with the Kitty keyboard protocol instead of sending a bare DEL. #13871 macOS: Pasting and dropping text now prefer plain text over URLs, so a path copied from apps like Transmit pastes as a path instead of an sftp:// URL. #13152 #13170 #13212 macOS: The search bar keeps focus when you click in it or on the next/previous buttons, and the terminal's focus state is now correct while search is open. #11872 #11978 macOS: The Find Next and Find Previous menu items and the navigate_search and end_search keybinds now work correctly, including while the search field is focused. #12070 #12492 macOS: Pressing Enter in the search bar no longer blocks confirming an IME candidate. #12781 macOS: Clicking a command palette entry with the mouse now runs it instead of closing the palette. #11665 macOS: The command palette now gets focus and paste when opened from the inline tab title editor. #12524 macOS: Holding cmd+t to create many tabs now leaves the newest tab focused. #13725 #13985 macOS: Fix an empty "ghost" tab or window that could appear when a tab was closed right after it was opened. #12119 macOS: Titlebar tabs no longer disappear after creating a tab from "Show All Tabs". #12949 #13017 macOS: Double-clicking the window title now zooms the window with macos-titlebar-style = tabs . #12219 macOS: Moving a tab with macos-titlebar-style = tabs on macOS 26 no longer briefly shows the neighboring tab. #14847 macOS: The inline tab title editor stays in place while the window is resized. #12220 macOS: Fix tabs flashing when switching tabs after a program changed the background color with OSC 11, and the window chrome keeping the old color after a light/dark theme switch. #12825 #12828 #12822 macOS: The macos-glass-regular and macos-glass-clear options for background-blur now layer the glass over the background color, and focused windows are no longer less transparent than unfocused ones. #13914 #13928 macOS: The native titlebar no longer cuts off the end of the title when using a custom window-title-font-family . #14135 #14217 macOS: Fix terminals rendering at a stale size under heavy system load or during rapid resizes from window managers. #12143 macOS: Splits dragged into another tab or window now render immediately, and the source window keeps keyboard focus. #12343 #12338 macOS: The split zoom indicator no longer stays visible after the other splits of a zoomed split are closed, such as with AppleScript. #14703 macOS: The split divider now uses the standard row and column resize pointers. #13433 macOS: window-save-state = never now also stops macOS from taking window restoration snapshots, which could stall focus changes between windows. #14506 macOS: Window state saved by Ghostty 1.2 or later is now migrated, so windows and tabs are restored after updating Ghostty. #12461 macOS: Tabs created while the screen is locked now initialize correctly. #13639 macOS: Quitting now asks for confirmation when windows with running processes are minimized or the quick terminal is hidden. #13686 macOS: OSC 52 clipboard read confirmations no longer steal focus. If the terminal is unfocused, Ghostty rings the bell and shows the prompt when you return to it. #13744 macOS: Splits in the quick terminal now also set GHOSTTY_QUICK_TERMINAL=1 . #12895 #12896 macOS: The quick terminal no longer reopens at a stale size after a display is reconnected at a different resolution. #13250 macOS: The "New Ghostty Tab Here" and "New Ghostty Window Here" services now open the correct directory when given a plain-text path. #12727 #12731 macOS: Working directories passed from Services, Shortcuts, and AppleScript are now normalized, fixing Nushell and zsh %1~ prompts. #12614 #14051 macOS: ghostty -e no longer opens the command's file arguments as extra terminals, e.g. ghostty -e vim file.txt . #13748 macOS: Opening a .command file from Finder no longer corrupts non-ASCII characters in its path. #13862 macOS: The Shortcuts terminal entity now reports the correct kind, title, working directory, and screenshot for new terminals. #13007 macOS: The Shortcuts "New Terminal" action now works with commands that have arguments and with a command field that was cleared. #12391 #12392 macOS: AppleScript send key now works for character keys, not only special keys like enter , and respects macos-option-as-alt . #13205 macOS: Update pill fixes: update errors are now shown, "Install and Relaunch" no longer asks for confirmation, and the cancel option is hidden once an update can no longer be canceled. #13540 #13562 #13612 macOS: The default app icon follows the system icon style again after changing it in System Settings, and custom icons now apply to the app in Finder. #12180 #12344 macOS: The dock icon bell badge now appears when notification permission was granted earlier without badge permission. #12133 macOS: The Copy menu item is disabled when nothing is selected. #12521 macOS: Menu items now show the correct shortcut for keybinds on physical keys (e.g. super+backquote ), uppercase letters, forward delete, and the scroll_to_selection and search_selection actions. #13888 #12039 #12011 #12281 macOS: The secure input indicator's popover arrow now points at the icon. #12249 macOS: Fix a rare permanent freeze after waking from sleep or changing displays. macOS did not mark the app as "Not Responding", so it could only be killed. #14691 macOS: Fix a crash when closing a tab, most easily triggered with undo-timeout = 0 . #13359 #13364 macOS: Fix a crash when opening a new tab from a native fullscreen window. #13636 macOS: Fix a crash caused by a data race when reading cached terminal contents. #13646 macOS: Fix a crash when OSC 52 clipboard confirmation prompts overlap. #13648 macOS: Fix crashes when CoreText returns null, such as for fonts without a display name or under severe memory pressure. #13642 #13679 macOS: Fix closed windows leaking with transparent titlebars (the default), which made Ghostty and WindowServer use more CPU and memory over time. #13601 macOS: Fix a memory leak each time Ghostty reads terminal text, such as for copy, Quick Look, or accessibility. #12020 #12025 macOS: Fix an IOSurface memory leak when scripts rapidly create and close terminals. #13640 macOS: Fix a Mach port leak, and a gradual slowdown, while global keybinds wait for Accessibility permission. #13590 GTK (Linux, FreeBSD) GTK: Splits can now be rearranged with drag and drop, matching macOS. Drag a split by its handle and drop it onto another split, including splits in other tabs and windows. #10224 #10423 GTK: Ghostty now renders at the true fractional scale (e.g. 125% or 150%), so text and box-drawing characters are sharp instead of blurry under fractional scaling. #1938 #14269 GTK: The renderer no longer uses GtkGLArea . Ghostty now renders with EGL entirely on the render thread and hands finished frames to GTK as DMABUFs, so the main thread no longer does any OpenGL work. #14052 #14636 GTK: Windows can now be renamed using the menu, command palette, or the new prompt_window_title and set_window_title binding actions. #10469 #10999 GTK: A new +new-tab CLI command opens a new tab in a running Ghostty instance. When run from inside Ghostty, the tab opens in the same window. It accepts the same -e , --working-directory , and --title flags as +new-window . #11762 GTK: A new +toggle-quick-terminal CLI command toggles the quick terminal of a running Ghostty instance, useful for binding in window managers without global shortcut support. #12661 GTK: Global keybinds now use the vicinae-hotkey-v1 Wayland protocol when the compositor supports it (e.g. Hyprland 0.56+), falling back to the XDG desktop portal otherwise. Ghostty shows a desktop notification if a global keybind can't be registered. #13464 GTK: quick-terminal-screen is now supported on Wayland. The default, main , places the quick terminal on the compositor's primary output (or the first monitor if the compositor doesn't report one). Set it to mouse to let the compositor choose, which was the previous behavior. #11117 GTK: On Wayland, background-blur now uses the compositor-agnostic ext-background-effect-v1 protocol instead of KDE's blur protocol, enabling blur on compositors such as Niri. The blur region also no longer covers the window's client-side shadows. #10721 #10720 #10727 GTK: On GTK 4.23.3 and newer, background-blur uses GTK's built-in background blur, which covers the window more accurately. #13581 #13586 GTK: The open_config binding action now accepts new_window to edit the configuration in $VISUAL or $EDITOR in a new Ghostty window. The default, os_open , keeps the previous behavior. #11905 GTK: A new configuration gtk-horizontal-tab-scroll (default true ) can be set to false to stop two-finger horizontal scrolling from switching tabs, passing the scroll to the terminal application instead. #12659 GTK: A new configuration gtk-tabs-inverted moves the close button to the start of each tab, in both the tab bar and the tab overview. #14657 GTK: The default command palette entries are now translatable. #11641 GTK: The embedded Noto emoji fonts were updated, so newer emoji and ZWJ sequences such as the head-shaking faces render as one glyph instead of overlapping neighboring cells. #14047 GTK: ctrl+shift+page_up and ctrl+shift+page_down now move the current tab left and right ( move_tab ), matching Firefox, GNOME Terminal, and VS Code. jump_to_prompt moved to ctrl+shift+arrow_up and ctrl+shift+arrow_down . #4998 #12458 GTK: URLs now open through the XDG desktop portal, falling back to xdg-open if the portal is unavailable. Ghostty passes an activation token so the opened application, such as your browser, can come to the front on compositors that require one. #5991 #11754 #14785 #14787 GTK: Desktop notifications are now withdrawn when their terminal is focused or closed, and repeated notifications with the same text replace each other, matching macOS. #14108 GTK: Tabs that aren't visible no longer render, saving CPU and GPU. This matches macOS. #12760 GTK: The Dolphin "Open Ghostty Here" action now opens a new window in the running Ghostty instance instead of launching a separate one. #11614 GTK: Fix Ghostty sometimes failing to launch with systemd 262, which refused to start the service because Ghostty reported readiness before it could handle reload signals. #14398 #14399 GTK: Fix deeply nested splits sometimes becoming invisible or losing focus. #11193 #12698 GTK: Resizing splits, especially with resize_split keybinds, no longer flickers. #13414 GTK: resize_split on nested splits no longer causes large jumps in size. #12699 GTK: Splits can no longer be resized smaller than one cell, by dragging the divider or with resize_split . #14476 GTK: High-resolution scroll wheels no longer scroll much faster than standard scroll wheels. #12483 GTK: Disable unwanted kinetic scrolling on trackpads with GTK versions older than 4.20.1. #11793 GTK: Middle clicks are once again sent to terminal applications using mouse reporting when gtk-enable-primary-paste is disabled in GSettings. #12940 #13108 GTK: The quick terminal no longer breaks when toggled off manually while quick-terminal-autohide is enabled. #11679 #12471 GTK: Opening the right-click context menu no longer hides the quick terminal when quick-terminal-autohide is enabled. #12843 GTK: The resize overlay no longer keeps reappearing when the scrollbar is visible and no longer blocks mouse input while shown. #11970 #11972 GTK: The maximum window size is now based on the monitor the window is currently on, not the monitor it was opened on. #13171 GTK: +new-window -e now works when shell-integration is set to a specific shell. +new-window and +new-tab also accept a new --shell-integration flag. #12378 #13741 GTK: Keys remapped to modifiers with XKB (e.g. Delete remapped to ISO_Level3_Shift ) no longer also send the original key. #13967 GTK: On Wayland, the IME candidate window now follows the cursor while composing and no longer covers the line being edited. #14729 GTK: Splits in a tab that was moved to another window now act on the new window (e.g. toggle_fullscreen ). #14474 GTK: The mouse cursor keeps its text shape while selecting text. #14558 GTK: The command palette now uses the terminal colors when window-theme = ghostty . #14662 GTK: Opening URLs no longer fails when the fallback opener ( xdg-open ) produces large output. #12797 GTK: Clicking a desktop notification no longer focuses the wrong terminal when the one that sent it has since been closed. #12028 GTK: A bell in the focused terminal no longer leaves the bell indicator set. #13597 GTK: Fix the window continuously redrawing in the background after an indeterminate progress bar (OSC 9;4) was removed. #14704 #14738 GTK: Log missing or invalid gtk-xft-dpi values once instead of repeatedly. #14410 #14085 #14434 GTK: Fix a crash when closing tabs or splits on GTK 4.20 (GNOME 49). #12426 GTK: Fix a crash with global keybinds or on configuration reload when no D-Bus connection is available. #13101 GTK: Fix a possible crash when Fontconfig reports a font's language as a plain string instead of a language set. #14853 GTK: Fix a leak where every audio bell started a new GStreamer pipeline and threads that were never cleaned up, slowly raising CPU usage. #13647 #12815 #13657 Snap: Link the system FreeType, Fontconfig, HarfBuzz, libpng, and zlib instead of bundled copies, fixing frequent crashes caused by two copies of the same library in one process. #14392 #14682 Snap: The snap's own GIO modules and XDG data directories now take priority over the host's. #12045 Snap: Programs running inside Ghostty, such as clear , now find the xterm-ghostty terminfo entry. #12662 Flatpak: Commands started by Ghostty on the host are now terminated if Ghostty crashes. #12427 Localization Ghostty 1.4 introduces full localization for the command palette and adds support for 4 new languages : Basque Belarusian Danish Serbian (Cyrillic and Latin scripts) Localization is maintained by volunteer contributors. If you want to help localize Ghostty in your language, please open a discussion on the GitHub repo. Thank you to all the volunteers who contributed to Ghostty's localization! Changes for Package Maintainers Ghostty now requires Zig 0.17 to build. #14518 #14519 GTK builds now require GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7 , up from GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5. Builds against older headers fail at compile time, and Ghostty exits at startup if older libraries are loaded at runtime. #14330 GTK builds now link the system EGL library (pkg-config egl , usually provided by libglvnd or Mesa) for the new renderer. At runtime, Ghostty uses GTK's EGL display when it can, and otherwise needs an EGL driver that supports the surfaceless platform. #14052 #14636 A new -Dinstalled-exe-path build option sets the absolute executable path written into the desktop file, D-Bus services, and systemd user service. Previously this path came from the install prefix. Without the option, these files now name ghostty alone, which systemd only finds in /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin , so set it for any other prefix. #14805 #14806 When linking the system gtk4-layer-shell ( -fsys=gtk4-layer-shell ), version 1.0.4 or newer is now required. Ghostty no longer disables the quick terminal on older versions, which can crash on some compositors. #11559 Libghostty As with 1.3, libghostty isn't directly part of the Ghostty 1.4 release. But a large part of the 1.4 development cycle went into libghostty, so here's an update. Over the past 6 months, the C API for libghostty-vt has grown from a parser and a few encoders into a complete terminal emulator API, adopted by dozens of free and commercial terminal emulators used by millions of people. It's hard to quantify exactly, but the number of people using a libghostty-based terminal is confidently several times the number of people using the Ghostty GUI. libghostty-vt now builds for macOS, Linux, Windows (MSVC and GNU), FreeBSD, Android, iOS, and WebAssembly, and CI continuously verifies every one of these targets. The goal is for libghostty-vt to be generally usable everywhere, within reason, so if you want more target support, let us know! It's also easier to integrate libghostty-vt into existing build systems. There's CMake support, Nix packaging, an xcframework, and a source tarball, in addition to the existing pkg-config file. libghostty-vt no longer needs libc++, and it can build freestanding. The API is still marked as a work in progress and broke compatibility several times during this cycle, so expect more breaking changes before a tagged release. The API documentation and the Zig, C, C++, Swift, and WebAssembly examples (now over 30) are kept up to date with main . We're going to do a final pass over the C API, break ABI one more time, and then likely tag a libghostty 1.0 release very soon. Financial Update Ghostty is a non-profit project , fiscally sponsored by Hack Club . All of our finances are public on HCB , so you can see exactly where every dollar goes. During the 1.4 cycle, we paid $41,820 to contributors under contract and spent about $1,260 on infrastructure such as website hosting. I'm happy to share that we've now signed our first two 12-month contracts , which give contributors stable, long-term paid work on Ghostty and help ensure the ongoing stability and sustainability of the project: @trag1c is Ghostty's head of operations. He manages the community on GitHub and Discord, coordinates our volunteer translators, and maintains various other important project systems. @vancluever works on various Ghostty subsystems. In this cycle, he led the upgrade to Zig 0.16, moved the build off Zig's deprecated @cImport , updated the bundled Fontconfig, and more. He's also the author of z2d , the 2D graphics library Ghostty uses to draw box-drawing characters and other sprite glyphs. If you'd like to support Ghostty, please visit our sponsorship page . Roadmap The primary focus of the roadmap continues to be libghostty functionality, stability, and portability. During the last release cycle, I said I aimed to tag a libghostty release. We haven't done that yet, but I'm confident we will do so before Ghostty 1.5. libghostty is a project that continues to be the tide that lifts all boats. libghostty improvements tie directly to Ghostty GUI improvements as well as dozens of other large projects in the ecosystem. As more large projects adopt libghostty, libghostty tends to get more testing and attention, and this creates a cycle that yields the most gain for terminal emulators everywhere. macOS and GTK builds of Ghostty have talented, capable maintainer teams that are continuing to improve them, so they're not neglected by any means! As a project, we've decided to drop any roadmap for Windows support in the Ghostty GUI. libghostty fully supports Windows (and we test it in CI), and the official stance now is that downstream projects should use that. Our release cycle remains 6 months. This release was delayed by one month, but Ghostty 1.5 is planned for March 2027. libghostty will have a separate release cycle. Your browser does not support the video tag. Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. Your browser does not support the video tag. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. As part of exploring this capability, we have also been experimenting with Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 to bring our frontier research together with Gemini Robotics . In the example below, Argon breaks down a user-instructed task into steps for Genie to render. These steps are interleaved as text captions to Genie 4 as the simulation is rendering. Because Genie 4 can be steered in real-time with text captions using Gemini, this now unlocks the path of adapting the simulation as it progresses towards the completion of that task. This capability becomes a path for simulating a breadth of scenarios in imagined worlds, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4. Your browser does not support the video tag. Learnings from trusted testers While Genie 4 is a major research milestone, it remains an early, experimental model. To understand how interactive world models can support real-world workflows—and where they still need to grow—we’ve been working with cohorts of trusted testers across creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering. Testers highlighted how the leap in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering allows ideas and concepts to be turned into realistic simulations, unlocking new abilities across disciplines: Creative direction : Creatives and technologists are testing Genie 4 as a rapid "draft mode" for pre-visualization and ideation. For example, filmmakers can step into a live simulation of a scene and run multiple "takes" in real-time, adjusting camera angles, lighting, dialogue, and action on the fly. Historical scenarios & immersive photographs : Photojournalists are exploring how a single 2D archival photograph can become a grounded simulation of that environment in seconds. Teams are testing how populated, dynamic worlds can help experience historical spaces or visualize how short-term environmental events, like a flash flood or wildfire, unfold. Interactive experience concept design : Game developers and creative technologists are testing Genie 4 to go from an initial idea to an explorable prototype in seconds, testing visual styles, material aesthetics, and interactive mechanics through natural language prompts before writing a single line of engine code. Simulation : Aside from our robotics research, enterprise partners across industries are evaluating Genie 4 as a tool for rapid "zero-to-one" scenario generation, and identifying gaps to further improve Genie to best fulfill that simulation need. Future Work: Towards hybrid world models A promising path for future progress lies in hybrid world models, which combine the logical, structured reasoning of code and language models with the rich, sensory representation of pixel-level simulation. Bringing Genie and Gemini models closer together is an early step in this direction. Gemini works behind the scenes to map the structure and plan the narrative timeline, while Genie generates the immediate physical reality—rendering how the world looks, sounds, and responds, pixel by pixel. Together, these complementary strengths can unlock a new class of world models that are far more coherent, controllable, and grounded than either approach could achieve alone. Building world models responsibly Genie 4 marks a new area of frontier research that merges real-time generation and photorealism, introducing a new range of capabilities and dimensions that we want to roll out and explore in a responsible way. Genie 4 includes strict safety guardrails that are consistent with our safety policies across other models. Before launching this preview, we evaluated Genie 4 through internal rigorous safety evaluations to prevent the generation of harmful or malicious content. Also, we have intentionally deployed it first to trusted tester partners to get early feedback, before we release the model more broadly. To maintain transparency, all video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, our imperceptible digital watermarking technology that helps identify AI-generated content across visual and audio modalities. Understanding current limitations Genie 4 remains an early, evolving area of research. While it can maintain coherent environments over short sessions, visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time—especially as a simulation runs longer, after multiple complex prompt edits, or when navigating throughout the scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, rendering legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are active areas of ongoing research. We are sharing Genie 4 as a preview to learn alongside our community and safely advance the frontier of interactive simulation. Next steps for Genie 4 Genie 4 has been released as a research preview to trusted testers, and is coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . We’re excited for users to step inside, experiment, and build their own interactive worlds soon. A programmer can point at any line of code and see who wrote it, when, and what the file looked like on any past day. A lawyer reading a federal statute usually cannot, at least not without an afternoon in the notes at the foot of the section. But why shouldn't they have the same, convenient system of record? It is especially relevant given that so much first-pass legal research now runs through language models, which are often unable to utilise the proper lineage of a law, handcuffing its ability to offer interpretation. The US code Outside the titles Congress has enacted as positive law, the code is only prima facie evidence of the law, and the Statutes at Large govern where the two differ. [ 1 ] The Office of the Law Revision Counsel publishes it as a series of release points, each current through a named public law, and keeps reorganising it; a bill to enact title 41 as positive law was introduced in September 2025. [ 2 ] Which public law wrote a sentence is recorded in amendment notes, in prose. When a change took effect is often in a separate effective-date note, and where Congress said nothing the default rule is that a law takes effect on the day it is enacted. [ 3 ] The definition of a small business debtor in 11 USC § 1182(1) shows how far apart those answers can be. It was created in 2019 with the existing small business debt limit. [ 4 ] The CARES Act raised the limit to $7.5 million in March 2020 as a temporary measure, later extended to March 2022. [ 5 ] , [ 6 ] That increase lapsed on 27 March 2022, and on 21 June 2022 Congress restored it for two more years, for cases commenced on or after 27 March 2020 and still pending, which reached back over the gap. [ 7 ] The higher limit expired again in June 2024, and after the triennial adjustment in April 2025 it stands at $3,424,000. [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] For a case filed in May 2022, the release point printed at the time gives the lower limit, and only a later Act changes the answer. A history that is useful to a lawyer has to carry the text, the date each change took force, and the scope of any law that reaches back. A study from the Technical University of Munich this year found two failures in models answering questions on German statutes: they apply rules that were superseded after their training cutoff, and they prefer the newer provision even when an older one governs the facts. One model answered 24% of post-cutoff questions correctly on its own and 87% when the relevant statutory text was retrieved for it, and the authors conclude that temporal validity has to be treated as a hard constraint. [ 10 ] Other recent work trains search agents to respect the date a question is about, with large gains in consistency. [ 11 ] Asking a model to produce the old text does not solve this. When the same Munich group had a model apply German amending laws to earlier versions, the output looked 93–99% similar to the official text, but only half of single amendments and a fifth of chains of amendments matched exactly, and experts found legally significant errors in the near misses. [ 12 ] The history has to be checkable. For each pair of release points from 2017 onward, we took the public laws enacted in between, carried out their amending instructions on the older text in date order, and compared the result with the newer version. Of 365 changes across the nine titles, 361 reproduced the next release point exactly. The other four are shown with a label saying how far they could be confirmed. Each change then carries the law and the date it took effect: 261 took effect on enactment by default, 72 by an effective-date note and 29 by a date in the amendment itself. One depends on an agency determination that may never come, and we leave it out of the text rather than guess. With that record, the reader can answer the questions lawyers ask. You pick a date and get the text in force on it, with the words that read differently today marked. Each phrase is coloured by the Act that wrote it. A change to a defined term lists every other provision that uses it, and you can follow a section to see what has changed since your last visit. Limits It does not yet show a later law’s reach back on the earlier dates it covers, so for a case filed in the 2022 gap it shows the lower limit without warning that the June 2022 Act changed the answer. Effective-date notes are read by pattern, and unusual wording falls back to the date of enactment. Each change links to the law’s own words, and for anything that matters the original should be read. We're also still thinking about the right form factor this should take. Sign in it’s a small world after all Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest Ole Bielfeldt of Germany captured a microscopic view of an inkjet printer depositing ink onto paper. Jennifer Ouellette – Oct 22, 2026 3:34 pm | 39 Credit: Ole Bielfeldt Credit: Ole Bielfeldt Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries. Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents’ attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying , his photography and videography brand. It was Bielfeldt’s curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera’s shutter speed. Bielfeldt’s solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques. “Ole Bielfeldt’s winning image embodies what makes Nikon Small World so powerful: the intersection of microscope imaging, ingenuity, and artistry,” said Eric Flem , a spokesperson for Nikon Instruments. “By using a microscope objective in a different way, he transformed a familiar object into something altogether new and previously unseen. It is a reminder that the microscope is not only a scientific tool but also a creative one, capable of expanding how we see and imagine the world around us.” Founded in 1974, the Nikon Small World competition celebrates its 52nd anniversary this year. In 2011, the company added the Small World in Motion competition (see the 2026 winner here ). Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope. Here are the top 10 winners of this year’s competition; the full list, with honorable mentions, can be found here . Nikon is also producing a full-color 2027 calendar featuring the 2026 winners. title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
body_text: Survival LLM An AI that still works when the internet doesn't. Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer. Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from. Download for Mac 212 MB Download for Windows 25 MB Source code Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none. What it does Works with no internet The AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it. Shows its sources Every answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted. Made for emergencies Medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles. Pick your version The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More memory means a smarter model. Your computer AI model it uses Our emergency test Model download Mac with 128 GB or more memory NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super 21 of 22 right 80 GB Mac with 32–96 GB Qwen3.8 27B 21 of 22 right 18 GB Windows PC with 32 GB or more NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 19 of 22 right 25 GB Mac or PC with 16–31 GB IBM Granite 4.2 8B 14 of 22 right 6 GB "Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library ( how we tested ). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check. Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or 1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one). Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11. Set it up in three steps Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading. Download Survival LLM for Mac or Windows and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All . Open it. On a Mac, double-click Survival LLM . On Windows, open the extracted folder and double-click Survival LLM.bat . Follow the setup. The app opens in its own window and downloads the AI engine (built into the Mac app), the AI model that fits your computer, and the library. Let it finish while you're online. The first time you open it, your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store. Mac: click Done , open System Settings > Privacy & Security , scroll down to "Survival LLM was blocked", click Open Anyway and confirm with your password. You only do this once. Windows: click More info , then Run anyway . What's in the library Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second: About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles WikiMed medical encyclopedia MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information) WikEM emergency medicine Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides CDC travelers' health U.S. military medicine and survival manuals Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates wikiHow how-to guides iFixit repair guides Appropedia (appropriate technology) Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange) Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the full list with licenses . Good to know It can be wrong AI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check. Private No account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off. Your own files Add PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer. Updates Check for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your models, library and files. Battery On a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily. Update notes Already have it? Click Check for updates at the bottom of the app. 0.3.4 October 27, 2026 Reasoning setting: next to Send, choose how much the AI may think before it answers: Off, 1,000, 4,000 or 16,000 tokens, or no limit. At the limit its thinking stops and it answers from what it has, so a model stuck reasoning in circles still answers. It replaces "Think harder". When the AI looked things up but never wrote an answer, it now gets the best articles it found and tries once more, instead of showing nothing. Thanks to betsyisaac for finding this. Ask it to look something up and it searches the library, even if it first answered from memory. Answers say whether they came from memory, from articles it read, or from search results it didn't open. A warning when Reasoning or Length limit is set to no limit. 0.3.3 October 27, 2026 Mac: quitting with Cmd+Q now also stops the AI engine and frees the memory its model used. Before, it kept running in the background. Thanks to wigginthethird for the report and the fix. Library search no longer shows several copies of the same page, so the AI sees more different articles. Thanks to ahalekelly. 0.3.2 October 27, 2026 The AI no longer saves your question as a memory note. Some answers no longer open with a made-up "Sources:" line that listed the AI's search commands instead of articles. Show reasoning reads more clearly: it says when you stopped it, the time shown is how long it thought, and long reasoning scrolls with the page. Windows: cleans up an empty folder that earlier updates could leave behind. 0.3.1 October 27, 2026 Show reasoning: under each answer, open what the AI thought before it answered, with the searches and articles it read in between. It stays hidden until you click it. Most models reason first only when Think harder is ticked. 0.3.0 October 26, 2026 Memory: tell it about yourself, like a family member's allergy or the generator you own, and it keeps a short note for later chats. See and edit every note under Memory , or turn its saving off. Downloads now work on computers whose network or antivirus uses its own certificates. All releases on GitHub Survival LLM is open source (MIT license). Code, library tools and source attributions: GitHub .

title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
body_text: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dhruv Mehrotra Maddy Varner Dell Cameron Security Oct 28, 2026 4:00 PM Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents The leaked records include the locations of ICE and CBP facilities, workers’ cell phone numbers, and the members of groups tied to wiretap programs, Palantir software, and xAI’s Grok chatbot. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. The DHS and DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents , including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119 , a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool. “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.” Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: Go inside the world of digital security with Kernel Panic We sexted with a Muse AI agent —and Meta says that’s totally fine Big Story: Meet the DEA’s premier crypto detective OpenAI is pissing off mathematicians Want better search results? Make WIRED a preferred source in Google Written by WIRED Staff Topics immigration Department of Homeland Security Immigration and Customs Enforcement Customs and Border Protection privacy cybersecurity First Amendment free speech hackers hacking Read More ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations is engaged in far-reaching spying against left-wing activists that rivals the FBI and CIA crackdowns on the Civil Rights and anti-war movements. Ali Winston UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech A government watchdog is considering a probe into the Home Office’s use of ChatGPT technology to process asylum claims amid concerns over the tools’ accuracy and secrecy surrounding their use. Isabella Ward ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud Documents obtained by Democracy Forward show that ICE looked into feeding voter roll data into the ELITE tool, normally used to identify targets for deportation. David Gilbert ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity in Maine, but stored information about them in a database run on Palantir software, newly unsealed court filings say. Maddy Varner Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy As a recent government report on DOGE shows, even getting basic information out of the Trump administration will put a new Congress to the test. Vittoria Elliott Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls From heat maps to Signal chats to war rooms, volunteers across the US are ready to act if federal immigration agents show up on Election Day. David Gilbert The Secrets of a US Spyware King In an exclusive interview with WIRED, Paragon Solutions CEO Andrew Boyd reveals the limits of the company’s promise to keep bad actors from abusing its powerful espionage tool. Kim Zetter AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals Anti-cybercrime initiatives are increasingly using AI to scam the scammers by tricking them into talking to lifelike bots that they think are real victims. Lily Hay Newman A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There Despite the agency's human resources department saying he hadn’t even been onboarded, Jeremy Lewin oversaw the destruction of USAID. It’s not clear he had the legal authority to do so. Molly Knight Raskin An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office Chatbot prompts reveal the engineer’s alleged efforts to set up a covert listening device days before one was found in a meeting room used by high-level executives. Paresh Dave A Mysterious Nonprofit Run by SpaceXAI’s Top Lawyer Is Paying the Salaries of Government Workers The National Design Studio has been something of a successor agency to DOGE. A WIRED investigation finds some of its members are on loan from a nonprofit run by SpaceXAI’s general counsel. Vittoria Elliott Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists Despite Illinois’ sanctuary laws, local police in and around Chicago helped ICE investigative agents track activists engaged in First Amendment–protected activities. Ali Winston WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. Through rigorous investigations and game-changing reporting, we tell stories that don’t just reflect the moment—they help create it. When you look back in 10, 20, even 50 years, WIRED will be the publication that led the story of the present, mapped the people, products, and ideas defining it, and explained how those forces forged the future. title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees
body_text: [script_0] Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A on the Way? - bret.dk Home News Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4… Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 2 Launched – Generative… Pineberry Pi to Pineboards with 4 New Products! Libre Computer Big Cottonwood: What we know so… MangoPi H616-based MQ Quad Released Reviews Radxa Dragon Q8B: A Laptop Cosplaying as an… Raspberry Pi CM0 & EDATEC CM0NANO – Raspberry… ArmSoM AIM7 Review: RK3588 Meets Jetson Nano Raspberry Pi 500+ (Plus) Review & Specs: NVMe,… Sunfounder Pironman 5 Review: A Feature-Packed Raspberry Pi… Benchmarks Raspberry Pi microSD Card Performance Across The Pi… Flirc Raspberry Pi 5 Case Review Raspberry Pi 5 Review 9.5 Best Raspberry Pi 5 microSD Cards Libre Computer Alta Review (Big Cottonwood) Pi Guides Raspberry Pi 5 Operating Systems: Complete Guide to… Site-to-Site VPN Guide: UniFi Router to UpCloud Installing Frigate on Raspberry Pi 5 with a… Installing PyCoral for Google Coral on Raspberry Pi… How to configure the Google Coral Edge TPU… About Support The Site Contact Me Search Home » Raspberry Pi » Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A on the Way? Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A on the Way? by Bret 27/10/2026 Published: 27/10/2026 Last Updated on 28/10/2026 11 minutes read 146 Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed ( Phoronix also spotted it ), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot. Table of Contents Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down? Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A How Do They Compare? What We Don’t Know (Yet) Thoughts Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down? The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my  Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks  piece covers the jump from the original pretty well. The headline from the  Zero 3 W device tree  is the SoC. It’s the  Broadcom BCM2711 , the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the  Raspberry Pi 4 , replacing the  Zero 2 W’s  quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at how those two compare on sbc.compare . That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back. Beyond the SoC, here’s what else stood out to me: eMMC on a Zero?  The storage controller is configured with an 8-bit bus width and a comment describing it as driving “the eMMC/SD card”, which only really makes sense for eMMC. I’d love to see it, but I’m not expecting it to make the final board, as it’d push the price up on a range that lives and dies by its price tag. My money is on this being a leftover or an option kept open during development, and microSD being what we get. An SPI flash bootloader.  The GPIO names include SPI flash lines, which suggests the Zero 3 W gets the same EEPROM-based bootloader as the Pi 4 (the Zero 2 W never had one). That should bring the Pi 4’s boot options along with it, and the ability to  update the bootloader  in the usual way. A single HDMI output , with the second HDMI controller permanently disabled. No surprise there given the form factor. A power button  defined on GPIO 46 and mapped to KEY_POWER, so we may be getting a physical button (or at least a header for one) much like the Pi 5. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth  wired up in the same way as the rest of the BCM2711 family, with a single ACT LED for status. The usual 40-pin GPIO layout  (GPIO 0-27 with the ID EEPROM pins), so your existing HATs should be fine. There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath. Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A The second surprise is a  Raspberry Pi 4 Model A . We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see! No Ethernet.  The Ethernet controller isn’t enabled anywhere, and the GPIO lines that drive the Ethernet PHY on the Model B have been repurposed. Very much in keeping with previous Model A boards. A single HDMI output  rather than the Model B’s dual micro HDMI. No 3.5mm audio/composite jack.  The analogue audio pins are empty and the composite video encoder is disabled, so audio will be over HDMI (or USB/I2S if you’re that way inclined). microSD only , with the same 1.8V signalling support as the Model B for the faster UHS card modes. External antenna support.  This is the one I find most interesting. There are two antenna control lines (ANT_CTRL1 and ANT_CTRL2) and overlay parameters named  ant1 ,  ant2  and  noant , which is exactly how the Compute Module 4 switches between its onboard antenna and an external U.FL connector. If that carries over to the final board, it’d be a lovely addition for anyone sticking a Pi in a metal enclosure. PWR and ACT LEDs , the same SPI flash bootloader setup as the Model B, and the same power button definition as the Zero 3 W. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here. The previous Model A, the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A from 2017 How Do They Compare? Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright. Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W Raspberry Pi 4 Model A Raspberry Pi 4 Model B SoC Broadcom BCM2711 Broadcom BCM2711 Broadcom BCM2711 CPU Quad-core Cortex-A72 Quad-core Cortex-A72 Quad-core Cortex-A72 HDMI 1x 1x 2x micro HDMI Ethernet No No Gigabit Wi-Fi/Bluetooth Yes Yes, with antenna switching* Yes Storage microSD (unless..) microSD microSD Analogue Audio/Composite No No Yes (3.5mm) SPI Flash Bootloader Yes* Yes* Yes Power Button Yes* Yes* No LEDs ACT PWR, ACT PWR, ACT What We Don’t Know (Yet) Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either. Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the  1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch ), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0. Thoughts On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board. Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto sbc.compare as soon as I can get one in my hands. Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments!
