title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware threatens most servers on planet Earth
body_text: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth - Ars Technica Skip to content Ars Technica home Sections Forum Subscribe Search AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Feature Reviews AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Forum Subscribe Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Pin to story Theme HyperLight Day & Night Dark System Search Sign In Sign in dialog... Sign in BREAKING THE CHAIN OF TRUST Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth Critical flaw in EDK2 allows attackers to execute code early in the boot process. Dan Goodin – Oct 27, 2026 4:25 pm | 74 Credit: Getty Images Credit: Getty Images Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process. The cat has left the bag The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week. With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language. “This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).” CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted. As the official advisory puts it: During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length. The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges. Yet another forever day CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail , stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw. Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include: PKFail , a supply-chain failure resulting from non-production test platform keys, public for more than a decade before they were discovered, used in hundreds of device models BootHole Bootkit and BlackLotus Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems. There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear. “For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars. “Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.” CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default). In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code , however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation… for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well. Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2. While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them. Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond. Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting. Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. In his spare time, he enjoys gardening, cooking, and following the independent music scene. Dan is based in San Francisco. Follow him at here on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. Contact him on Signal at DanArs.82. 74 Comments Staff Picks A Autapomorphy See, patching PHP last week would have been pointless anyway. This sounds a lot less apocalyptic than PHP due to the additional requirements for exploitation. This requires that: 1. The system is in PXE boot. That requires both that PXE boot is enabled for the system and that the attacker hits a window of seconds when the computer is watching its network adapter for PXE traffic. 2. The attacker can reach the computer with ICMP traffic in this window. A great proportion of Internet facing resources are sitting behind some sort of front-end service, be that CloudFlare or various sorts of load balancers. If you ping the address for such a system, it's the front-end that answers those ICMP messages without delivering them to the back-end server. The PHP thing was a vulnerability in a system that's intentionally exposed directly to Internet traffic and that's available 100% of the time, which made it far more exploitable. The other thing that will really help with fixing this is that there need not be any extra service downtime. The fix is in the firmware, so patching needs only to set the firmware up to perform a capsule update on rebooted. The reboot itself can be delayed until one next happens normally. title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
body_text: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course Subscribe Sign in Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. Sebastian Raschka, PhD Oct 24, 2026 358 14 37 Share I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers. We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates. Topics covered Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code 5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture). The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision. The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model. Topics covered Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties Implementing a simple heuristic scorer Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures) Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500 Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code 6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training. Topics covered Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code 7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail. Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards. We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful. Topics covered Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code 8. Distilling a reasoning model Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop. We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning. Topics covered Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1) Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code Final words As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind. For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of different ideas similar to the suggestions in the exercises. And if you would like the full written walkthrough, figures, and exercises alongside the videos, you can find Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) at Manning and Amazon . title: A Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting
body_text: The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting Skip to main content Search This Blog Metadata On distributed systems broadly defined and other curiosities. The opinions on this site are my own. The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting Get link Facebook X Pinterest Email Other Apps - October 26, 2026 I have come to suspect that to most people thinking is painful. Some of us are addicted to thinking. Some of us find it a necessity. Johnny enjoyed it. I even have the suspicion that he enjoyed almost nothing else. -- Edward Teller, eulogizing John von Neumann I listened to Ananyo Bhattacharya's " The Man from the Future: The Visionary Life of John von Neumann " in my car during the many commute hours Bay Area traffic afforded me. I thought I should share the Johnny phenomena here. I knew about von Neumann being a very influential mathematician/scientist/engineer but the full list still left me bedazzled. In his 53 years of life (1903-1957), von Neumann seeded so many fields. Every time there was an important discovery in physics, mathematics or computation, John von Neumann was there. Set theory and the foundations of mathematics. The mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics. Operator algebras (still called von Neumann algebras). Ergodic theory. Game theory. Expected utility theory (which is the foundation of most of modern mathematical economics). The Monte Carlo method. The stored-program computer architecture that every machine you have ever touched is built on. Numerical weather prediction. Fault-tolerant computing. Self-reproducing automata (cellular automata), and arguably, the logical structure of molecular biology, four years before Watson and Crick. There is also, unfortunately, the implosion lens for the Nagasaki bomb, and a decade of hawkish nuclear strategy. Early years At six, Janos (the OG hungarian name for Johnny) could divide eight-digit numbers in his head and hold a conversation in ancient Greek. He later added Latin, French, German, English, and Yiddish.  The rumor was that he remembered everything he ever read. Many years later Herman Goldstine decided to test this by asking him to recite "A Tale of Two Cities." Von Neumann started on chapter one and had to be asked to stop fifteen minutes later. Budapest around 1900 produced an absurd cluster of minds: von Neumann, Eugene Wigner, Edward Teller, Leo Szilard, Paul Erdős, Theodore von Kármán, George Pólya. When several of them turned up at Los Alamos and realized they had gone to high school together, Szilard joked that Hungary was a cover story for a Martian landing. But even inside the Martian cluster , von Neumann was the outlier. Wigner, a Nobel laureate himself, was asked at Los Alamos to explain the Hungarian phenomenon and said there is only one phenomenon that is worthy of explanation, and that phenomenon is John von Neumann. The cluster may be less mysterious than it looks: Budapest was one of the few genuinely welcoming places in Europe for Jewish families, and it pushed them toward the professions the nobility considered beneath them, mathematics among them. The schools then did the rest, with a nationwide math competition and top quality high school teachers. As for the Johnny phenomenon, from the pedagogical perspective, the following stood out to me from Johnny's early years. The first is the dinner table. Von Neumann's father Miksa (Max), a lawyer turned banker so successful that the Emperor ennobled him for service to the national economy, ran the evening meal as a seminar. He would start by going through his own day: the cases he argued, the deals he negotiated, whatever was on his mind. Then each of the three boys would present on what they had been reading. The whole family would then argue about Heine's poetry, or antisemitism in Europe, or the paradoxes of omnipotence. Sometimes Max would bring home business clients, and the boys were allowed to grill them about whatever they wanted funded. Frequent guests included the director of Budapest's Theoretical Physics Institute and one of Freud's students. The second is the languages. Max knew the good times could end, told his sons so explicitly, and wanted them able to survive anywhere in any language. He was preparing them to flee. He was right. When John was fifteen, the communists took over Hungary and targeted rich families like his. A few months later the counterrevolutionaries beat the communists and then massacred thousands of Jews for supposedly collaborating. The von Neumanns survived by leaving the country at the right moments, and possibly by being too rich. Johnny's first ten years included no formal schooling at all, because organized primary schools were not a tradition there yet. He had governesses, private teachers, and his father's enormous library, and he apparently used it to memorize a 44-volume German history of the world, which he would later deploy to freak people out at parties. Finally, when he did get to the Fasori Gymnasium at eleven, the math teacher, László Rátz, concluded fairly quickly that he could not teach this kid and arranged a private tutor. The tutor was Gábor Szegő, who went on to chair the math department at Stanford. Szegő is said to have come away from the first lessons in tears at what the boy could already do. The results of this tutelage showed up a couple years later. At seventeen Johnny gave a new definition of the ordinal numbers, where each number simply is the set of all the numbers before it. Zero is the empty set. One is the set containing zero. Two is the set containing zero and one. And so on up into the infinite ordinals, with nothing but the empty set and a pair of braces to build from. If you think about it, this is a very computer-science-y way to define numbers: an inductive datatype with one constructor.  He pushed this further in his doctoral thesis a few years later. Set theory at the time was still suffering from the paradoxes, Russell's set of all sets that do not contain themselves being the famous one. Johnny's fix was essentially a type system for sets: the ordinary ones you can put inside other sets, and the oversized ones you can talk about but never use as an element. The paradox then becomes a type error. Note that it is the same abstraction move in both times: take an object everyone thinks they understand, and replace it with the smallest thing that behaves the same way. Johnny kept doing the same thing in field after field for the next thirty years: arrive, find the smallest set of objects and axioms the mess is actually about, write them down so that everyone can finally argue about the right thing, and then leave before the theorems fell out. Teller said Johnny enjoyed thinking, but I think the addiction was much more specialized than that. His real superpower was " the art of abstraction ". Look at the list from the introduction again with this in mind. Matrix mechanics and wave mechanics looked like rival theories until he noticed they were two coordinate systems on the same Hilbert space. Economists thought comparing preferences across people was hopeless until he asked what minimal consistency axioms a chooser has to satisfy, and derived a cardinal utility scale from them in an afternoon. Self-reproduction looked like it needed an infinite recursion of blueprints until he separated "read the tape as instructions" from "copy the tape as data." Making quantum mechanics rigorous Having finished his PhD at 21, Johnny arrived at Göttingen at 22 because it was the world capital of mathematics, under Hilbert. The timing couldn't have been better. Heisenberg, one year older, was down the hall having just invented matrix mechanics. A year later Schrödinger produced wave mechanics in Vienna. The two gave the same answers and implied completely different pictures of reality, and physicists were uneasy with both: matrices were unfamiliar mathematics then, and nobody could say what the waves were. Von Neumann's first move was to prove the two were the same theory in different forms. Then he wrote "Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics" (1932), which set the whole thing up rigorously in Hilbert space. The author of the book Bhattacharya, who did physics as an undergrad, points out that this is still the most watertight formulation we have.  Once the math was clean, the measurement problem became more visible. Where does the wave function actually collapse? At the apparatus, the detector, the retina, or the conscious observer? Von Neumann declined to take a position, but proved it does not matter mathematically where you draw the line because the answer comes out the same. That line is now called the von Neumann cut. Game theory and economics Nothing much came of game theory until von Neumann proved the minimax theorem in 1928, in his early twenties. Every two-player zero-sum game has a solution: either a strategy one player can pursue to win, or a mixed strategy with randomness in it (e.g., rock-paper-scissors). Then he lost interest and wandered off, as was his habit. He came back when Oskar Morgenstern turned up at Princeton. Morgenstern, an economist, was stuck on what is essentially a liveness bug in economic modeling: you intervene in an economy, people adjust their behavior in response, which invalidates the model you used to design the intervention, so you build a new model, which they also adjust to. An infinite loop. Morgenstern had concluded that all attempts to model economies must fail, which made him unpopular right up until the Wall Street crash made him look prescient. Von Neumann had the tools to attack the problem. Over about eighteen months they produced the 600-page "Theory of Games and Economic Behavior" (1944) and founded the field. Johnny did this as a hobby. During those same years he was designing implosion lenses at Los Alamos and building the first programmable computers. He would drop in on Morgenstern for a long session and then vanish back into the rest of his life. Two things from this work are still everywhere. The first is the axiomatization of expected utility. Putting human preferences on a cardinal scale and comparing them across people was considered more or less impossible, and von Neumann sat down one afternoon and did it. This relates uncomfortably with the longtermism material from the Cal Newport/Émile Torres conversation I wrote up recently . Expected value math is a hell of a drug. The second is its limited model. His framework is built on zero-sum games and on coalitions: given n players, which coalitions are stable? Most of his book is about that, but a lot of the world is not zero-sum. Nash's non-cooperative equilibrium , which generalizes minimax, is what opened that up, and von Neumann rejected it essentially out of hand when Nash walked into his office. To him it was a trivial step, a fixed-point argument he could see through instantly. He misjudged the importance of the non-cooperative approach. Bhattacharya flags a nice irony here: von Neumann, the alleged Cold War hawk and the model for Dr. Strangelove, built a theory centered on people talking to each other and forming working coalitions. It was Nash, who had trouble with people, who formalized everyone optimizing alone. All models are wrong , but some are useful. The computer In 1944 Johnny ran into Herman Goldstine on a train platform at Aberdeen, found out about the ENIAC, and attached himself to the project. In 1945 he wrote the " First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC ", laying out the stored-program architecture: one memory holding both instructions and data, a control unit, an arithmetic unit, I/O. That is now the architecture of virtually all computers, from the desktops to smartphones, eighty years later. Von Neumann was adamant that the technical details go into the public domain, and circulating that draft is exactly what made the architecture unpatentable. So Johnny was also an early proponent of Open Source. He did the same with the IAS machine design, which got copied worldwide and produced a run of machines with goofy names: MANIAC at Los Alamos, JOHNNIAC at RAND, ILLIAC at Illinois, SILLIAC in Sydney, WEIZAC in Israel. For a man who gets painted as the cold rationalist hawk, putting the foundational design of the computing industry into the commons on purpose is a generous act. He also, with Ulam, invented the Monte Carlo method , then needed random numbers for it and had to invent pseudorandom generation. And he put the first serious application on these machines himself. The IAS Meteorology Project ran the first computerized weather forecast in 1950. Numerical weather prediction, and by extension climate modeling, is a von Neumann production. Reliable organisms from unreliable components In 1952 von Neumann gave a lecture series at Caltech titled "Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components." The vacuum tubes of the day failed constantly, and the standard engineering response was to make better tubes. His response was to ask whether you could build an arbitrarily reliable machine out of components that are guaranteed to fail, using redundancy and majority voting, and then to work out how much redundancy you actually need. That is one of the founding ideas of fault-tolerant computing, and gives rise to replicated state machine, quorums, and Paxos. Self-reproducing automata In the late 1940s, Johnny started asking what it would take for a machine to build a copy of itself . The naive worry is infinite recursion: the machine needs a blueprint of itself, and that blueprint must include a blueprint of the blueprint, and so on down forever. His solution (worked out with Ulam's suggestion to set it in a discrete cellular framework) was to split the role of the description. You have a universal constructor plus a tape describing it. The constructor reads the tape as "instructions" and builds the described machine. Then it copies the tape as uninterpreted "data" and attaches the copy to the offspring. One description is used twice in two completely different modes. This is the stored-program idea again, three years after EDVAC: the same bits are instructions when you execute them and data when you copy them. He published this in 1948 and 1949. Watson and Crick published the structure of DNA in 1953. So von Neumann derived, from pure logic, the necessary architecture of biological reproduction. That there must be a stored description. That it must be read in two distinct ways. That this separation is precisely what makes open-ended evolution possible. Translation and transcription. Genotype and phenotype. He got the shape of the answer years before anyone knew what the molecule was. The 29-state cellular automaton he built to prove it was also, incidentally, the first cellular automaton. Conway's Game of Life, Wolfram's entire research program, artificial life, and a foundations of what people now call synthetic biology all descend from his formal model. "Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata" was published posthumously in 1966. His last work, also published posthumously, was "The Computer and the Brain" (1958). In it he observes that the brain achieves what it does with terrible arithmetic precision and enormous parallelism, which is the opposite of the machines he had just finished building. There he argues that whatever language the nervous system computes in, it is not mathematics as we understand mathematics. We are still working on this last one! Personality Johnny loved parties, loud music, and fast cars. He drove crowded roads like a maniac, and got bored and slowed down on open ones. He wrecked a car roughly every year, usually a Cadillac, "because no one would sell me a tank". An intersection in Princeton was christened Von Neumann Corner for the number of accidents he had there. One of his accident reports says: "I was proceeding down the road. The trees on the right were passing me in orderly fashion at 60 miles an hour. Suddenly one of them stepped in my path. Boom!" He also did his best work in chaos, and played German march music at volume in his office at Princeton, generating complaints from neighbors who included Albert Einstein. His detractors called him cold, calculating, and ruthless. He did not join the Manhattan Project colleagues who agonized afterward, and instead he pushed the government toward bigger hydrogen bombs. He advocated an immediate preemptive nuclear strike on the USSR: "If you say why not bomb them tomorrow, I say why not today? If you say today at five o'clock, I say why not one o'clock?" Very brutal. And he said it in public, more than once, to journalists, while sitting on the Atomic Energy Commission. But notice that, this is rooted in his abstraction habit. Model the Cold War as a two-player zero-sum game, assume the Soviets get the bomb soon and would use it, and minimax says strike first. The math checks out, but the problem is the very simplistic model he uses. Stanislaw Ulam, who worked beside him for twenty years, put it as kindly as it can be put: "There was perhaps an inclination to take a too exclusively rational point of view about the cases of historical events." Paradoxically, the same man was remarkably generous with people. He moved heaven and earth for those he thought were promising: Turing and Mandelbrot both benefited, and he mentored David Blackwell, a Black statistician Princeton did not want, and pushed until they took him. Blackwell wrote later about how much it mattered. Johnny put his own reputation on the line testifying for Oppenheimer, whose politics he did not share. A friend described him as "always gentle, always kind, always penetrating and always magnificently lucid." Teller said: "Von Neumann would carry on a conversation with my 3-year-old son, and the two of them would talk as equals, and I sometimes wondered if he used the same principle when he talked to the rest of us." Which brings me back to the Teller line I opened with: Johnny enjoyed thinking, and Teller suspected he enjoyed almost nothing else. That is a lovely thing to say about a man at his funeral. It is also the setup for the cruelest possible ending, and Teller knew it when he said it. The cancer, probably from the radiation he absorbed standing around at weapons tests, started in the bone and went to the brain. He had spent fifty years as the fastest mind in any room he entered, and he had to watch that go. Teller: "When [Johnny] was dying of cancer, his brain was affected. I think that he suffered from this loss more than I have seen any human to suffer in any other circumstance ". Johnny remained a game theorist to the end. After a lifetime of culturally Jewish atheism, he asked to be baptized. His daughter attributed it to Pascal's Wager: a small probability of a much better afterlife, against a trivial cost.  Can we survive technology? In 1955 von Neumann wrote an essay called "Can We Survive Technology?" He spends most of it on nuclear war, but he touches on global warming. In 1955! And a few years earlier, in a conversation Ulam recalled in his obituary, he had already coined "singularity" (yes, that singularity ) for a point where technological progress accelerates past the possibility of predicting what comes next. This is what he actually argues about whether you can solve this by banning the dangerous technology: In looking for a solution, it is well to exclude one pseudosolution at the start. The crisis will not be resolved by inhibiting this or that apparently particularly obnoxious form of technology. For one thing, the parts of technology, as well as of the underlying sciences, are so intertwined that in the long run nothing less than a total elimination of all technological progress would suffice for inhibition. He goes on to say that a ban would have to be worldwide to work, and prohibition of invention runs against the entire ethos of the industrial age, and is not going to be heeded anyways. So what does he offer instead? What safeguard remains? Apparently only day-to-day — or perhaps year-to-year — opportunistic measures, a long sequence of small, correct decisions. [...] For progress there is no cure. Any attempt to find automatically safe channels for the present explosive variety of progress must lead to frustration. The only safety possible is relative, and it lies in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment. And then he names the qualities required: "patience, flexibility, intelligence". So, here is von Neumann, the master of abstraction, with no abstraction to offer. Maybe through his bout of applying minimax reasoning to nuclear strategy, he learned what a formal model is worth when the assumptions are shaky and the stakes are civilizational. book-review Get link Facebook X Pinterest Email Other Apps Comments Post a Comment Popular posts from this blog The Safest Job from AI may be Writing - August 31, 2026 Today, tech folk are scrambling to change their workflows to meet newly inflated 5X productivity quotas, while getting pummeled under the cognitive debt of agent-generated code. title: US Government is hiding a secret court ruling about how it spies on Americans
body_text: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dell Cameron Security Oct 26, 2026 10:09 AM The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant. Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September. The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year. Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6. “If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED , “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.” Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability. The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.” Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.” Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay. Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers. Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year , after the department approved a rebuilt version. This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April , citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.” While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling , cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna . None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.” According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “ not possible to track .” Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.” Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March , “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.” The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March. Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it. title: Solar power is becoming bigger than nuclear
body_text: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jocelyn Timperley Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here. The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s. Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember . And BBC analysis of Ember data over the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power. "[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here. 1. An underestimated force "Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK. Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history , and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly). That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones "It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year . Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong". Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold. Ember/ BBC Ember data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC) 2. 'Offensively cheap' Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further , says Jones. "Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow. In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all." Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022 . 3. Global uptake China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player. Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar , it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024 . In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households . "Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland. "However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines ." Getty Images China's internal solar boom is now slowing down, but its cheap solar exports to other countries are still increasing (Credit: Getty Images) India, meanwhile, is moving away from fossil fuels far faster than China did, and new solar has met 60% of its rise in power demand in the past two years. In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households. 4. Unreliable fossil fuels Countries like Pakistan and Lebanon have also begun installing solar at breakneck speeds , while across Africa countries are installing some 100,000 solar panels per day. In many places, escalating diesel prices, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and US-Israel war with Iran , has swung the cost needle yet further in solar's favour. This is especially the case in many African countries where home diesel generators are a mainstay due to unreliable grids. Rooftop solar panels, nearly all of them imported from China, have now taken off as an alternative. Ethiopia has even banned the import of petrol and diesel cars in a bid to tackle oil dependency and pollution, says Jones. Solar is also rapidly providing new electricity where fossil-based grids can't keep up with demand. Pakistan, for example, has become a surprising poster child for the solar revolution due to its extraordinarily rapid rise in installations . In 2019, solar provided less than 2% of its electricity; now it's 24%, driven by costly, unreliable grid electricity combined and cheap solar imports from China. "What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans." A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria . "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable." 5. Battery revolution Solar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries. Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution , transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening." Alamy Solar has gone from Pakistan's fifth-largest electricity source in 2023 to its largest in 2025, says Rosenow (Credit: Alamy) In California, for example, solar and batteries met on average over a quarter of electricity demand from 19:00-21:00 (the evening peak) over the first half of 2026. US states such as Vermont are now rolling out grid-integrated systems of home batteries, often paired with solar. Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow. 6. Electrify everything Solar is seen as a key part of the push towards electrification , reducing fossil fuel use in areas that previously didn't use electricity, such as via electric cars. Electrification has been chosen as a major theme at this year's UN climate talks in Turkey . "That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones. Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently . "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient." The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up." In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority . "Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government." 7. Expanding tech In the past few years, plug-in panels (or "balcony solar"), have started spreading rapidly in Germany . These generate less electricity than rooftop panels but feed it directly into homes via a standard socket. They have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California . Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar. Getty Images In Kentucky, US, a solar ranch pays a local farmer to graze his sheep among its solar panels, producing pasture-fed meat while keeping grass and weeds down (Credit: Getty Images) Other technologies from floating and "mirror" solar plants to perovskite panels and solar windows could all see growth in coming years. What's next for solar In 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones. This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations , leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones. By 2030, the IEA thinks solar power generation will have reached double that of 2025's levels, with solar overtaking hydro to become the world's third-largest electricity source . "Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed." More like this: • The US state replacing power plants with home batteries • The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit • Perovskite: The 'wonder material' that could transform solar There has been a lot of bad news about the climate recently. It's now incredibly likely the 1.5C global limit set in Paris in 2015 will be breached, the world is seeing rising climate impacts and is edging towards several climate tipping points this century. But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built. "Now, worst cases [of climate change] are somewhere between 2-3C of warming, rather than 4C of warming." -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week.
