Content from Discoverable Servers Easier to Discover Kelsey Duncombe-Smith October 27, 2026 Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord, with at least 1,000 members. Their admins chose to list them in Server Discovery so anyone can join them, no invite link needed. Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord. Admins and members can decide if and how their content is shared, and those controls start rolling out today, ahead of any changes. TL;DR: Help people find your community with Server Web Pages. A Server Web Page is a page on the web that describes a Discoverable Server, so people can decide whether they want to join. Starting November 16, 2026, all Discoverable Servers will have a Server Web Page. These pages may also display summaries of discussions happening in public channels (those visible to everyone in the server), to give a better sense of what people are talking about. Some messages from public channels may show on Server Web Pages and in web search beginning in mid-December 2026. The rollout is gradual, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages start appearing on the web. Server admins can opt channels out starting today, before anything goes live on November 16, 2026. Controls for admins are in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or opt all channels out. If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, and your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026, if you don't already have one. Users have control over whether their messages are shown. If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off starting today in User Settings > Data and Privacy , before messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026 (or anytime after). One setting covers Channel Messages in every Discoverable Server. Channel Summaries are generated separately, from broader channel topics, and will still appear on Server Web Pages unless admins choose to turn them off. Usernames and avatars won't be shown alongside messages on Server Web Pages Private servers, DMs, and GDMs are always private and not included in these changes. These changes are limited to Discoverable Servers. How servers work today Over the years, Discord has built different kinds of spaces, so every group can decide how big the party gets and who can find it: Most servers are small, private spaces. They're meant for you, your friends, and nobody else. Community Servers are for bigger groups , with the tools to handle a crowd. Though someone still has to send you an invite link. Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord . To qualify, a server needs at least 1,000 members, has to be at least eight weeks old, and must meet activity and safety requirements . Anyone can find and join them, no invite link needed. Today’s announced features only apply to this type of server. Today, there are more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers, spanning communities from speedrunning to language learning to niche corners of every fandom. People find their way into communities they'd never have stumbled across otherwise. Until now, that's all being Discoverable meant. Why this matters Server Discovery was built for finding servers, not answers. Ever wanted to look up tricks for a faster speedrun? Or whether a powerful item is worth grabbing, or if it will completely ruin your build? Someone has almost certainly already answered it in a channel somewhere, in one of 63,000 Discoverable Servers. It can just be hard to find. Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios. These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this. By giving admins the option to make certain channels discoverable from the web, we can help more people find and benefit from the knowledge shared in Discord communities. We expect this to help different types of communities in various ways: For fandoms, you can make specific channels an easy-to-find resource that answers the top questions new players ask. For content creators, you can more easily promote events and new content drops. For indie game developers, you can use public channels, including forums, to share updates and wiki-style information about your games. What's new for Discoverable Servers? Server Web Pages live on the open web and give people a glimpse of what a Discord community is about before they join. They’ve been available to Discoverable Servers for some time, but setup takes a few steps, so not every Discoverable Server has created one. Learn more about Server Web Pages . Starting from November 16, 2026, every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page. If you’re an admin and have already set one up, you don't need to do anything. If you don’t have one and want to get a head start on how your community shows up to the rest of the internet, you can go through the setup process today and publish it in a few clicks. If your moderation team doesn't set one up beforehand, a default page goes live for you on November 16, 2026, using details from your Server Profile. You can edit it whenever you like. Having a Server Web Page is a core part of being a Discoverable Server. If you don't want one, you can always switch back to being a Community Server . Server Web Pages are also getting more useful. Until now, your Server Web Page has shown a small description of what your community is about. From November 16, 2026, it may also start showing what your community is talking about. Including this helps someone with a question find their way to your community if it already has the answer. Channel Summaries. These show a small slice of what's being talked about in your server, directly on your Server Web Page. These automated summaries focus on active conversations from November 16, 2026, onwards. Admins can change which channels they draw from, curate the summaries that are shown, or turn them off entirely. Usernames and avatars will not be shown in summaries. Channel Messages. From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words. Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages. You can already see an early version of this on a few Server Web Pages. We’ve been piloting Channel Messages with Discoverable game communities, including NBA 2K , Rust , and Dead by Daylight . (During this pilot, all posts were from admins and moderators, not members.) If you're running a community, useful answers to common community questions can show up in web search: how to unlock an easter egg, new builds or strategies, or a boss guide. Someone looking for help will be able to find a real answer from a real person, and can step straight into the conversation that it came from by clicking through and opening Discord. What does this mean for Discoverable Server members? Starting mid-December 2026, if a server’s admins allow it, messages from public channels can appear on Server Web Pages and in search results, without usernames and avatars. Messages you sent before then won’t be shown. Channels where content may appear on the web will be labeled, so you know before you send a message. If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off today in User Settings > Data and Privacy . One switch covers every Discoverable Server you're a part of. We're rolling this out gradually, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages from those channels go live. Learn more . What can admins do now? Your server controls start rolling out today , in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or turn them all off. If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026 (if it's not already published), and Channel Summaries can start the same day. Channel Messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026. You can adjust your Channel Summaries and Channel Messages settings before they roll out. And if you'd rather publish your Server Web Page yourself, you can do that today. See the full details in our Help Center . However you set things up, we hope this is a step toward bringing back what made forums great: answers anyone can find, and an open door to the community that wrote them. Frequently Asked Questions How will I know if I am in a server that allows content to appear on the web? Discoverable Server admins choose which channels to make available on the web.Those channels will be labeled, so you’ll know before you send a message. As always, you can customize your own privacy choices in your user settings under Data & Privacy. What if I decide later that I don’t want my messages shown on the web? You can turn off your Channel Messages setting anytime in User Settings > Data and Privacy . Messages you send after that won’t appear on the web. Messages you sent while it was on stay up unless you delete them from Discord. Messages from before mid-December 2026 aren’t included, regardless of your setting. Learn more . Does this work the same way in every region or for every user? ‍ In the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting for Channel Messages is off by default given legal restrictions, so members’ messages won’t appear on the web unless they turn it on. Users in the teen age group are excluded completely and cannot enable Channel Messages until they’re an adult. Everywhere else, it’s on unless members turn it off. Other than that default, everything works the same way in every region. Learn more . Tags No items found. It won't fix your bug. It'll fix you. Every other tool hands you the answer; Nietzschian Debugger hands the question back. You paste your bug. It doesn't fix it. Instead, it: Challenges your assumptions about what's happening Forces you to confront the evidence you're avoiding Attacks the assumption you're proudest of — the one you stopped questioning Guides you to the fix yourself — your realization, not the AI's Why? AI is making developers weaker. Copy-paste from ChatGPT, ship, repeat. Nobody understands their own code anymore. Nietzschian Debugger forges stronger developers — through struggle, not shortcuts. This isn't anti-AI — it runs on Claude, on purpose. It's anti- outsourcing-your-thinking . Every other tool uses the model to hand you the answer; this one uses it to hand the question back. "He who has a why to debug can bear almost any how." Installation # Python 3.10+ pip install nietzschian-debugger nietzschian debug " your bug " No API key yet? See it in action first — no key, no cost: nietzschian demo Note: the current tool is the Python package above. The old npx nietzschian-debugger serves a stale pre-rewrite build — it has been deprecated in favour of the pip install. Requirements: Python >= 3.10 An Anthropic API key (BYOK) — or bring another model (OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, …), or run a local Ollama model, which needs no key. See Models — set one up, switch any time . Setup Set your Anthropic API key: # Linux / macOS export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= " sk-ant-... " # Windows (PowerShell) $env :ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = " sk-ant-... " # Windows (CMD) set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... Quick Start # Start a debugging session (adaptive by default — it reads your state and shifts lens) nietzschian debug " My API returns 500 but only on Tuesdays " # Force a single lens instead of adapting nietzschian debug --lens socrates " My login endpoint fails randomly " nietzschian debug --lens zarathustra " Memory leak in production " # Point it at specific code nietzschian debug " Auth fails in ./src/middleware/auth.ts " # Interrogate your actual uncommitted changes (feeds the git diff as context) nietzschian debug --diff " tests started failing after my last change " # Use any model — Claude by default; or OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, local Ollama… nietzschian debug --model ollama:llama3.1 " my function returns null sometimes " Models — set one up, switch any time Claude is the default and the sharpest experience. With ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, every command just works with no flags. But the tool is model-agnostic — it speaks the OpenAI API, so almost any hosted or local model works too. Switching models The model is chosen per command with --model . There's no config to edit and no state to reset — you switch just by changing the flag, or drop it to return to Claude : nietzschian debug " my bug " # Claude (needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) nietzschian debug " my bug " --model openai:gpt-4o-mini # a hosted model nietzschian debug " my bug " --model ollama:llama3.1 # a local model, no key The flag isn't sticky — each run is independent. (There's no mid-session switch yet; to change model, re-run the command with a different --model .) Hosted models (bring your own key) Set the matching key, then select the model: export OPENAI_API_KEY=... # or GEMINI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY, … nietzschian debug --model openai:gpt-4o-mini " ... " nietzschian debug --model deepseek:deepseek-chat " ... " nietzschian debug --model gemini:gemini-1.5-flash " ... " Supported: openai, gemini, deepseek, groq, mistral, together, openrouter, xai — plus custom:<model> with NIETZSCHIAN_BASE_URL for any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Local models with Ollama (no key, no cost, offline) # 1. Install Ollama (https://ollama.com) and make sure it's running # 2. Pull a model once: ollama pull llama3.1 # 3. Add the provider deps once, then point the tool at it: pip install " nietzschian-debugger[providers] " nietzschian roast ./messy.py --model ollama:llama3.1 (LM Studio works the same way: --model lmstudio:<model> .) Which local model should I use? Different jobs reward different kinds of model — and the twist is that the best model for predict is the worst for roast : Command Best local model Why roast , debug a general chat model — llama3.1 , qwen3 built for prose and wit predict a coding model — qwen2.5-coder it wants a precise function call — exactly the dare A coding model asked to roast reaches for JSON instead of a joke; a chat model asked to predict is vaguer about the exact return value. Match the model to the job. Honest caveat: the "never give answers" discipline is sharpest on Claude . Smaller local models leak and over-ask more — the built-in validator and the roast/predict guards catch a lot of it, not all. Share a session Your sessions are made to be shared. Turn the last one into clean markdown: nietzschian share # most recent session, to your terminal nietzschian share -o run.md # or save it to a file Three Lenses — it picks, not you By default it adapts : each turn it reads where you are and shifts between three methods. You don't choose a difficulty — a confused developer can't diagnose their own state, so the tool reads you instead. Nietzsche is home; it shifts only on sustained signals, not twitchily, and the active lens shows in every turn header ( [Turn 3 · socrates] ). When you're… Lens What it does confused — you don't know what you mean socrates Relentless clarification. Defines your vague terms until a testable claim appears. The stingray, not a gentle mentor. avoiding — hiding in an assumption nietzsche The tuning fork. Taps the idol you're proudest of and listens for the hollow ring. defeated — ready to quit zarathustra Affirmation. Reframes the bug as the weight that makes you stronger, and will not let you quit. None of them is soft — adaptivity changes the angle of the blade, never sheathes it. To pin one lens instead of adapting: nietzschian debug --lens socrates " my bug " nietzschian debug --lens zarathustra " my bug " How a Session Looks $ nietzschian debug "login endpoint returns 403, but only for users who signed up before last week; new signups work; same code path; Node/Express" Nietzschian Debugger [Adaptive mode] [Turn 1 · nietzsche] You said "same code path" — but the data is screaming that something changed between last week and today. What is different about the user record itself between those who signed up before last week and those who signed up after? > I assumed the records were identical. Let me actually compare one. [Turn 2 · nietzsche] "Assumed." There is the word you built a week of debugging on. Stop assuming and read two rows side by side. What field exists on an old account that a new signup was never given? > ...the old ones carry a legacy role claim the new ones don't, and the auth middleware rejects any token without it. [Turn 3 · nietzsche] There it is. The bug was never in the code — it was in your certainty that "same code path" meant "same data." You stopped looking exactly where the difference lived. > found it Session Complete -- 3 questions to root cause (Solved) Your Debugging Profile: ┣ Assumption-checking ████████░░ strong ┣ Evidence-gathering ██████░░░░ moderate ┗ Root cause speed ████████░░ strong "Man is something that shall be overcome." -- Friedrich Nietzsche Or when you call a test "flaky": $ nietzschian debug "integration test passes locally but fails in CI — it's flaky, I just rerun until it's green" Nietzschian Debugger [Adaptive mode] [Turn 1 · nietzsche] "Flaky." The word you reach for when a test has found something true and you'd rather it hadn't. A test that fails one run in three isn't random — it's telling you something is ordered that you assumed was not. What does CI have, or do in a different order, that your machine does not? > idk, maybe the database isn't ready yet [Turn 2 · nietzsche] "Maybe" — you named a suspect and refused to question it in the same breath. A database that wasn't ready would throw a connection error, not a wrong answer. Unless your test is reading rows another test wrote. Do your tests share a database, and are they guaranteed to run in order? > ...they share one. locally they always run alphabetically [Turn 3 · nietzsche] There it is. "Flaky" was the mask on a race you refused to see — two tests fighting over the same rows, hidden on your machine by an accident of alphabetical ordering that CI parallelizes away. The test was never flaky. It was honest, and you were not. Will you isolate the data, or keep rolling the dice until they fall green? > oh. found it Session Complete -- 3 questions to root cause (Solved) Your Debugging Profile: ┣ Assumption-checking ███████░░░ strong ┣ Evidence-gathering █████░░░░░ moderate ┗ Root cause speed ████████░░ strong "No victor believes in chance." -- Friedrich Nietzsche Prove You Understand It — predict debug interrogates a bug. predict interrogates you : it dares you to say what one of your functions returns, then runs the code for the truth — never a model guessing (that can be confidently wrong). At the end it names the pattern in your misses, not a score. nietzschian predict ./parsers.py # 3 dares by default nietzschian predict ./parsers.py -n 5 # go five rounds $ nietzschian predict ./parsers.py Nietzschian Debugger [predict mode] 3 rounds — type 'quit' (or press Ctrl+C) to stop early. ── Round 1 of 3 ── You named it truncate, and now you believe it truncates. Sweet certainty. But look — you gave length a default of zero, and zero is a falsy little god that answers "if not length". So tell me, prophet: what does truncate("hello world") return? your prophecy > "" — it truncates to zero, so nothing Wrong, and gloriously so. "if not length" caught your zero and handed back the text untouched, before a single character was cut. You read the name and never the first line. The guard fired; your logic never ran. The truth, once run — it returned 'hello world'. ── Round 2 of 3 ── You wrote dedupe, and I can smell the doubt — most who write it reach for a set and let the order rot. Did you keep the order, or did you betray it? what does dedupe([3, 1, 2, 1, 3]) return? your prophecy > [3, 1, 2] Right — and not by luck. You kept the first sighting of each and dropped the echoes. Clean. There was no trap here; some things you simply know. The truth, once run — it returned [3, 1, 2]. ── Round 3 of 3 ── A tier function, a border drawn at one hundred. Borders are where confidence goes to die. Stand on the line itself and tell me which side claims you: what does shipping_tier(100) return? your prophecy > "freight" — 100 is the heavy tier Wrong. "weight > 100", and one hundred is not greater than one hundred. You stood ON the boundary and assumed it pulled you across; it let you fall back to 'parcel'. The strict > you typed yourself is the thing you forgot. The truth, once run — it returned 'parcel'. Proof of Understanding Two of three — and the two you missed were cut from the same cloth. You read functions by their name and their happy middle, and walk straight past the lines that quietly decide everything first: the falsy default that returns early, the strict > that owns its edge. You trust what the code is *for* over what it *says*. Read the guards before the gift — the boundary is not an afterthought, it is the whole argument. It runs your code in a separate process with a timeout — your own functions, called the way you'd call them. It only picks functions it can invoke with simple literal arguments, and a function that raises is a legitimate answer (predict that too). Roast Your Code — roast For when you don't want a question or a fix — you want the truth, fast and funny. Point it at your worst file; it reads the code's cowardice and laughs. Fixes nothing. nietzschian roast ./legacy/utils.py $ nietzschian roast ./legacy/utils.py 🔥 Nietzschian Roast A function named `helper` wrapping a bare `except: pass` — you built a room with no windows and called it tidy. The bug you're hiding from in there is the only honest thing you've written all week. "Not by wrath does one kill, but by laughter." — Thus Spoke Zarathustra Session Commands Command Effect solved or found it End session — you found the root cause I give up Get one lifeline question, then exit exit or quit Abandon session immediately Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D Force quit Features Refuses to Hand You the Fix — Every response is a question. It's built to withhold the answer, and a model-judge double-checks each reply to catch it when it slips. Proof of Understanding — predict dares you to say what your code returns, then runs it for the truth (never a model guessing) and names the pattern in your misses. Nietzschian Roast — roast reads your worst file and burns it down in one or two lines. Fixes nothing. Deeply shareable. Real Code Reading — Reference a file path and it reads YOUR actual code, not generic examples. --diff feeds it your uncommitted changes. Any Model, Even Local — Claude by default; or OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Groq, and more — or a local Ollama / LM Studio model with no key and no cost. Try With No Key — nietzschian demo runs a full scripted session so you can see it before committing a key. Shareable Sessions — nietzschian share exports a session as clean markdown you can post. Adaptive Lenses — it reads your state each turn and shifts between Socrates (when you're confused), Nietzsche (when you're avoiding), and Zarathustra (when you're defeated). You don't pick the difficulty; it reads you. Growth Score — Track your debugging skills across sessions with visual bar charts. Session History — All sessions saved locally in .nietzschian/sessions/ for trend tracking. Sliding Context — Long sessions don't crash; older turns are transparently summarized. Development # Clone and install git clone https://github.com/DilawarShafiq/nietzschian-debugger.git cd nietzschian-debugger pip install -e " .[dev] " # Run the test suite pytest # Run the CLI locally nietzschian debug " test problem " Tech Stack Python >= 3.10 Claude API via the Anthropic SDK Click for the CLI, Rich for the terminal UI pytest for testing License MIT About It won't fix your bug. It'll fix you. The debugger that hands the question back instead of the answer. pypi.org/project/nietzschian-debugger/ Topics ai claude cli cli-tool critical-thinking debugging developer-tools education learning llm local-llm nietzsche ollama philosophy python Resources Readme MIT license Contributing Contributing Activity Stars 499 stars Watchers 0 watching Forks 17 forks Report repository Releases Packages Used by Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
body_text: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 Â· enlyth enlyth . posts tags rss Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 26 October 2026 Â· 2 min read #windows #gui Early investigation For a while Iâve been wondering about a silly question, which is, whatâs the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation. Given Windowsâ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old. Sadly, Windows 11 canât run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so weâre going to have to find something from the early NT era. I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe . So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11: At the time of this post, thatâs a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me. So I kinda thought âcoolâ, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older. Further efforts Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with todayâs executable format or API changes that came later in development. The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such: push hwnd ; 4 bytes of args call [ShowWindow] ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them add esp, 4 ; the 1992 caller removes them again Which would understandably cause the program to crash. There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the systemâs crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 . If you start the program, you get something like this: That is because, duh, my computer doesnât have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio: Pretty cool for a program thatâs almost 34 years old! What if we cheat? So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported. But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications. Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01: And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post. title: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible
body_text: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible - bitlog.com Skip to main content bitlog.com Jake Voytko's personal log of bits Home About me Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible Written by Jake Voytko on October 27, 2026 Software is degrading all around us, for obvious reasons. I've written about this before. All else equal, if you increase your code production by 10x but you don't reduce your error rate by a factor of 10, then your production app is buggier than it used to be. I've seen threads where people also have some nostalgia for the past: "software used to be better in the past" or "we've forgotten how to program like we used to" or "software quality has been declining for decades." And as someone who has used computers since 1990, I'm here to disabuse you of this notion. Software was horrible. Everything crashed all the time. Yes, there were great programmers like John Carmack who could keep the entire program in their head and iterate on thoughtful codebases over decades. No, they did not write a majority of the software that we used to use. Historical context Almost everyone in the world was on Windows. Windows peaked around a 95% market share, plus or minus a few percentage points based on your source. Yes, you probably knew someone with an iMac who would tell you that it was way better than a Windows machine, and they could prove it if anyone ever actually released applications for Macs. And yes, there were Linux distros like Debian where people could get real computing done [0] . But those were exceptions. Almost every computer user had a Windows machine and either an Intel or an AMD processor. And Windows had a lot of problems. There was one saving grace though: companies only got one chance to ship their software. At a certain point, it was going to be loaded onto a floppy disk or burned onto a CD or a ROM, put into a box, and mailed out. And that version had to work out of the box. So there was some quality floor that you couldn't slip below. How bad did it get? Here's a collection of things that I remember. This isn't linear; it's my collection of memories from 1990 and onward. Blue Screen of Death Windows had extreme stability issues for most of my childhood. Let me introduce you to the song of my people, the Blue Screen of Death. The blue screen of death in Windows XP, Vista and 7, courtesy of Wikipedia This was Windows' version of a kernel panic. It happened right when you were in the middle of something. Or maybe you were doing nothing. It didn't matter: the blue screen was coming. Your computer crashed for a lot of reasons. First, device drivers. If you bought some new peripheral like a joystick, it'd come with a floppy disk or CD with device drivers. You'd dutifully install them. The device drivers had the same function as they do today: they help the operating system understand how to interface with the hardware. This might get you thinking, "Oh wow, so they sent out the device drivers on physical media? You can't update a physical disk once you ship it. Surely they took extra care to get everything right." My friend, this could not be further from the truth. I'm sure there were good drivers and bad drivers. But in aggregate, they were buggy, and it only took one marginal device driver to destabilize your computer. The Windows operating system also had its own code quality issues back then, and would sometimes fail to fully reclaim resources from programs that exited. So your computer would slowly degrade over time until eventually the slow rot would take down your machine. All in all, your computer would just blink out of existence from time to time. It was a fact of life. Autosave Do you know what pairs really well with a computer that crashes all the time? Applications that don't autosave. Even better, applications with autosave that don't flush buffered writes and corrupt their save files. It was commonplace to get into the zone and work on a document for hours, and then suddenly you would get either a Blue Screen of Death, or a pop-up saying that your application had a problem and had to exit. And you'd scream and you'd double-click your document over and over, but it was no use. You had to start over. But there was a consolation prize. It was your turn to tell everyone, "I was working on a document for THREE HOURS! And then the computer crashed and I lost everything. It was all gone. I had to redo it." There was always that one asshole that was like "why didn't you save?" But you didn't get mad. You knew that he was 2 weeks from having the same thing happen to him. When I joined the Google Docs team back in 2010, we instrumented the Ctrl+s keyboard shortcut for fun. It didn't do anything but record a metric saying that it had been pressed. This "save" keyboard shortcut was in the top 5 non-editing user actions, just behind things like "move the cursor with arrow keys." And it did absolutely nothing. Google Docs autosaves. But everyone was so traumatized from years or decades of losing work that they reflexively saved anytime they edited anything. Nothing was secure When my sister and I were little, we loved going into stores with display units. The computers would often have games installed you could play. Worst case, you could always open up MS Paint or Solitaire and mess around for a few minutes. One time, we were in a store where the display models had password-protected screensavers. My sister was undeterred. She just hit Ctrl+Alt+Del, selected the screensaver application, and clicked "End Task." And we were in. The best minds of Microsoft were nothing next to the hacking talent of a 9-year-old. And this is the level of security that your computer afforded you. If you used the Internet for long enough, your computer would start to collect a bunch of advertising malware. When you turned your computer on, you would start to see pop-ups and pop-unders with random ads, even when you weren't using browsers. So you'd do another antivirus scan, or later on you could visit websites that could also run the malware scans for you. And not to mention the viruses that would drop the Internet to its knees once a year by doing trivial things like "adding a macro to a Word document that sends emails." Disk fragmentation Any techie can remember going to a nontechnical relative's house. In some dusty corner, they'd have an ancient Windows computer barely hanging on by a thread. It would literally take 20 minutes to turn on. You'd sigh and say, "let me fix this for you." You would open two programs. This would take about 5 minutes. The first program emptied cache files and the Recycle Bin. The second was Disk Defragmenter. Your computer slowly became unusable if you never saw this window. Back in the day, hard drives in Wintel boxes stored data with spinning magnetic platters. The hard drive had a retractable arm with a little magnetic reader, and it would read data by retracting the arm to the right position and then moving the disk to the start of a sector. But of course, as you add more and more files, the game of Tetris doesn't work, and the rest of your file doesn't neatly fit onto the disk before the next file's record begins. So your file would end up in two (or more) places on the hard drive. This was called fragmentation. A little bit of fragmentation was unavoidable, but if more and more files became fragmented then your computer became slower and slower until eventually Grandpa's computer took 20 minutes to start. Many modern filesystems, Windows' included, automatically handle defragmentation in the background nowadays. But Windows did not back then. You needed to periodically manually start the defragmentation process yourself. By the time I got into college, I discovered that Windows had a scheduler and could run Disk Defragmenter whenever I wanted, so I just left my computer on all the time and let it defragment at 5 in the morning. Phenomenal cosmic power, itty bitty memory Applications were heavily memory constrained, so programmers tried to save bits and bytes everywhere. This should have been invisible to me, but it wasn't. At one point I had a crappy video game version of Axis and Allies for the PC, released in 1998 [1] . Imagine Risk but World War 2. And the AI was really bad, and could generally be beaten easily. But the game had a major flaw: If a country had more than 255 units, the whole game would crash. And naturally the AI also loved to turtle, so it was common for the AI to have a territory with over a hundred units that was impossible to wear down. So because of this programming choice, the game was a race to wipe out the enemy before it could force a stalemate by crashing the game. This kind of thing happened all the time. During my first programming class in my freshman year of high school, one of our lessons was effectively, "here's why you all recognize numbers like 128, 256, and maybe 65536." Software came on unreliable physical media Even if the software worked perfectly, you might scratch your game CD and lose the ability to play it. Then you'd start asking your friends if anyone had a spare copy of Red Alert or something, just so that you could finally finish the single-player campaign. This wasn't unique to CDs. Anything physical could degrade. My half-brother had a NES game called Dragon Warrior or something, but the cartridge was corrupted and there was no way to leave the first room. And even if you kept all of your games in good condition, the contacts inside of the NES that connected the cartridge to the console could rust and fail. This kind of thing happened all the time. "But Jake, that's hardware and not software." All I'm saying is that y our software was fragile and it needed to be protected and preserved. It's not like you had the option for a physical disk or the online install and you chose the disk. By the nature of distribution, the software itself would degrade and rot away from you. Online games assumed good behavior One of the earliest online games I played was Diablo II, which means that I have seen the true heart of darkness inside of humanity. Online games have a strange problem: gamers often don't want to be together. They just happen to cohabitate a space. And Diablo II had a lot of design features that lent themselves to chaos: There were rampant client-side hacks. In PVP servers, people would use hacks to e.g. fire tracking arrows far beyond the range that they should have been able to. All item drops were equally available to everyone in the server. That means when you got close to killing an act boss, you and your party would transition from allies to rivals and spam click when the boss finally popped. If you had a corpse on the ground and died again, you'd lose everything you had equipped. People would try to force you to have a full inventory by dropping a bunch of cheap items onto your corpse, hoping that you'd accidentally pick up common items before picking up your corpse. Then you'd try to pick up your corpse. You'd only pick up some of the items. Then they'd kill you a second time and you'd lose everything that you managed to pick up. The game had a lot of item duping glitches. As you can imagine, this ruined the in-game economy since it became dominated by the duped items. And it enabled a lot of scams. They'd pretend that they just duped an item, and they'd wait for someone to ask how they did it. Then they'd walk the user through step-by-step, but one step would involve dropping your item on the ground and then the scammer would pick up the item. There was no guild system, but people still ran guilds. This means that there was no trusted way to identify guaranteed friendlies. Many of these were fixed by the time Diablo III came around. They had extra guards against duplicated items. Bosses gave players individual drops, so there was no competition for items when you killed bosses. And you didn't need to recover items from your corpse in a way that risked you losing items. These were all hard-won lessons. Turbo button I started using my family's computer around 1990 when I learned how to read. The computer was a beige 286 that sat on our desk with the monitor perched on top. It had a 5.25" floppy drive. It had a power button. It had a reset button. And it had a TURBO button. The TURBO button was supposed to be ignored most of the time, but you could press it when you needed to slow the computer's processor down. Why would you need to do that? Because IBM's first desktop computers ran on the 8088 processor at 4.77MHz [2] . It didn't stay this way for long. But there was a problem: many programmers wrote their applications with the assumption that computers had that 4.77MHz processor. Programmers synchronized animations, video game frame rates, and generally relied on the assumption that they were working with a fixed clock speed. If you used one of these applications on a faster processor, they would likely be unusable. Computer manufacturers devised a simple solution: add a TURBO button that would just slow your CPU down on demand. Whenever you ran into an application that had timing issues, just press that TURBO button and watch it slow down to a comfortable speed. I never needed to actually press the TURBO button in anger. My understanding is that most of the applications that benefitted from the TURBO button were games, and we only played newer educational games that didn't have these timing issues. When editing this post, I thought about dropping this section a few times. But can you imagine having an "Original iPhone" button on the side of your iPhone so that the Notes app could work? Good grief. Modern software isn't perfect Modern software isn't perfect. It's bloated. It's slow. It was written by too many people. It's too complex. It has too many cooks in the kitchen. And now, we're losing our grasp on how it works under the hood as we delegate more and more to the agents. But I'd never go back to the way software used to be written. Give me process isolation and online updates. Give me higher-level programming languages that abstract common pitfalls from C and C++. Give me game designers that handle timing using the system clock. Give me Steam and Windows Update. You can keep your old release process that fell by the wayside. Footnotes [0] From what I remember from trying to install Debian in my high school years, the most popular app on Linux was anything that could edit XF86Config . [1] I'm having trouble corroborating this anecdote with information I can find online. The details might not be exactly right. But this is what happened, to the extent that the memory survived 25ish years. [2] Not GHz, MHz! CSS-Tricks has a new owner
body_text: CSS-Tricks has a new owner! | CSS-Tricks Ad WordPress sites from those who know WordPress best. --> Skip to main content CSS-Tricks Since 2007 Articles Almanac Guides Links Newsletter Shop Account icon-account Search css-tricks news CSS-Tricks has a new owner! By Geoff Graham on Oct 26, 2026 NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. Ad --> This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news: CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again! Just to recap:  DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022  from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase. Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site. So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site. That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion. Do you, like, own the site now? Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while. I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of  everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time. How can you afford this? My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right. It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently. In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.  So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise,  please do reach out !  LOL, advertising. Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.  (And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!) LOL, courses. Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as  our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap . And yes, I do believe that  learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are  down across the board . It has to be done differently. There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.  Oh, and  the newsletter . That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus. What about publishing new articles? That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going. But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling. That also means the  guest writing form  is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit. I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can.  Unless it’s a slop submission , of course. Will you be writing most of the articles to save cost? Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight. I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or helping with sponsorships. I gag at the thought of titles, but  publisher  hits best for me. My fingers are in all the bowls, but my most important responsibilities are: Helping writers develop a voice, and giving them a platform to use that voice, so that they help others get a little better at their jobs. The best thing I can possibly do is help folks develop a voice and give them a stage to use it. It’s about community and culture building.  Publisher . That’s more my jam. Can I support you in some way? You totally can.  I put a little membership deal together  where you can join a members-only community on Discord along with some perks. Or check out the new shop . Or  purchase advertising  for your company. In the near-future you will be able to purchase the aforementioned course as well. Any little bit helps, of course. I squirm at the thought of asking for money, so there’s no pressure. Support doesn’t even have to be financial! We all know that content publishers need all the eyeballs we can get in these prompt-filled days. Things like  subscribing to the newsletter , sharing articles you like with others, clicking through from your RSS app, and checking out our sponsors are all very, very great ways to support us. I have so many thoughts about this. Yeah, me too. This post could go on and on. I’m an open book, though, and I’m happy to answer anything you might have in the comments. I know, so 2015, right? title: GPT-6.1 Terra
body_text: Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra From visual understanding to action From visual understanding to action A significant step up on factuality and coding Safety and alignment Pricing and availability From visual understanding to action A significant step up on factuality and coding Safety and alignment Pricing and availability Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra. From visual understanding to action We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a ~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks over three times faster than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. On MMMU-Pro , a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost. OSWorld 2.1 tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task. A significant step up on factuality and coding This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. Terminal-Bench 4.0 tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice. Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost. Safety and alignment As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra. GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the system card ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Pricing and availability Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-terra . Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens. 2026 GPT Author OpenAI Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 GPT-5.5 Safety Safety Approach Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Plugins (opens in a new window) Models (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. title: Roblox downloaded 145GB models from us (including adult content) without asking
body_text: Open3DLab • Roblox downloaded 145 GB of models from our sites (including adult content) without asking ⯆ Network Sites Open3DLab SmutBase SFMLab Discord Mastodon BlueSky OPEN3DLAB ⯆ Menu Browse Tutorials FAQ News Members ⯆ Account Create Account Sign in Roblox downloaded 145 GB of models from our sites (including adult content) without asking By Salaryman on October 26, 2026 Last updated on October 26, 2026 On 15 and 16 October 2026, a crawler that said it belonged to Roblox walked through almost every project on Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase, and proceeded to download complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects. 145.5 GB of our creators' work, downloaded for what we assume are AI training purposes. This post briefly describes what happened, what mitigations were taken, and what this signals for the community at large. A more detailed writeup outlining what we saw in our logs will be posted at a later time. What happened On Sunday the 18th of October, we noticed a crawler making a large number of requests to our sites and download infrastructure. The crawler sent the same user agent on every request, trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com) . It came from a single Amazon Web Services (AWS) address. It had read the main page of 18,926 projects, which is practically our entire catalogue, in 26,429 requests over a span of 34 hours. After pulling the project pages, it downloaded complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects, 145.5 GB in all, before suspending operations during the weekend. The downloads include 364 files (54.8 GB) from 224 projects on SmutBase, which hosts adult content only. With the SFMLab projects marked adult, 345 of the 712 projects (62.6 GB) are adult content. The main limiting factor in the number of files downloaded was the crawler's reliance on the free download servers, which have caps on speed limit and number of concurrent downloads. The crawler did not respect our robots.txt, (which it did retrieve), ignored our Terms of Service, (which forbid scraping), and defied the creators' licenses: 423 of the 712 projects are licensed for non-commercial use only. Within the sample it retrieved, it took adult projects at the same rate as everything else. Some examples include models of Eve from Stellar Blade , Mei from Overwatch , and a Horse cock dildo . Our response We found it on 18 October and blocked further attempts the same morning. The scraper had suspended its activity by that point, and we did not notice any scraper that weekend. We emailed the address in its user agent on 18 October and asked Roblox for comment. We have not had a reply. The crawler resumed scraping activity on October 19th, with all requests getting blocked by our servers. The scraper did not reduce its download attempts when faced with our blocks, and the scrapes seemed to fit neatly within office hours, only briefly pausing for an hour around lunchtime, and ending activity around the end of the workday (CEST). On the 20th, their scraper made its final return at 8:00, slowly tapering requests from lunchtime onward, likely in an effort to test our rate limiting. The requests stopped around 15:00. We sent another email to Roblox for questions, to which they again did not reply. Speculation This section contains our speculation and assumptions based on public information, and the information we noticed in our logs. Roblox has been building a "3D foundation model" since at least 2025.In March 2025 Roblox introduced Cube , which it calls its core generative AI system for 3D and 4D. The accompanying paper describes the goal as a foundation model for 3D intelligence. It lists character rigging among the things that model should eventually do, and generating characters and avatars as future work. Its first shape model was trained on roughly 1.5 million 3D assets from licensed and public datasets such as Objaverse, plus free assets from Roblox's own Creator Store whose creators had opted in. In February 2026 Roblox began rolling out "4D generation" built on Cube. The address in the user agent belongs to a researcher who is among the 40-plus authors of that Cube paper. The researcher's public professional profile says they are building a 3D foundation model at Roblox, and their earlier published work is on 3D reconstruction and real-time 3D rendering. We want to be clear: we don't suggest this researcher did anything on their own initiative or out of the ordinary for their job. A data-collection run like this is a company's decision, and the responsibility for it is Roblox's. But the profile says what the user agent says: the people behind this crawler build 3D foundation models. The "trellis2" in trellis2-data-sourcing may refer to TRELLIS.2 , an open 3D generation model Microsoft released in late 2025. It may mean the data was meant for training or tuning a model like it, or it may just be a project codename. We don't know. What we can say is that TRELLIS.2's published data toolkit contains no web crawler and no user agent, so this crawler and its label were written for the job. It is also possible that Roblox is re-using the Trellis.2 tooling for its own foundational model and it is re-using these scripts for its next model; the tools are open source. Our sites are full of things a 3D model-generation system needs and public datasets have relatively little of: complete, textured characters, many of them rigged, in the formats artists actually work in, each with a title, a description and preview images. Put together, we think the most likely explanation is that the crawler was collecting training or evaluation data for Roblox's 3D foundation model work. We can't prove it, and we don't know whether any of our creators' files ended up in a model. Roblox's track record This isn't the first time Roblox has been criticised for how it treats the people whose work its platform runs on, or for how it handles other people's rights. Young developers. In 2021 the games outlet People Make Games published a video investigation arguing that Roblox turns its young users into underpaid developers. By its calculation Roblox kept around 75% of the money spent in developers' games, against Steam's 30%, and paid creators in Robux, which they can only cash out once they've earned a minimum amount. Roblox declined to discuss its revenue share and payout minimums. (In September 2025 it raised its cash-out rate by 8.5%.) Copyright. In 2021 the US National Music Publishers' Association sued Roblox for at least $200 million over unlicensed music on the platform. The case settled later that year for an undisclosed amount. Child safety. In October 2024 the short seller Hindenburg Research accused Roblox of inflating its user numbers and of failing to protect children. Roblox called the report misleading and pointed out that its authors stood to profit from a falling share price. Since then the attorneys general of Louisiana , Kentucky, Texas and Florida, among other states , have sued Roblox over child safety, and private lawsuits have been consolidated in US federal court. These are allegations, not findings. None of this proves anything about the crawler, but it strengthens our opinion that Roblox is a deeply unethical business. It shows a company that has repeatedly been accused of putting growth ahead of the people its platform depends on. You see how this looks, right? More than a third of Roblox's daily users were under 13 in 2025, by its own figures. Its rules ban sexual content, and in 2025 it tightened them further . Roblox's crawler took 224 projects from a site called SmutBase, which describes itself as exclusively for adult content, and 121 more that are marked adult on SFMLab. It took them at the same rate as everything else: 345 of the 712 projects it downloaded from are adult content. The further scraping attempts did not discriminate between adult content either. We want to be careful here. We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else. Models reproduce what they learn from. If adult training data reaches a model that generates assets for Roblox, the only thing between that data and children is whatever filter Roblox builds afterwards, because its data collection didn't filter anything. Furthermore, when a creator deletes a project, or we remove one for breaking our rules or after a copyright notice, it's gone from our sites, but remains in these datasets. One project the crawler took has already been disabled on SFMLab since. If Roblox still has its copy, that copy is still there. We're not against adult content. It's our bread and butter. We think consenting adults should be able to access and enjoy this content freely, without the government looking over their shoulder. What we object to is our adult sites being emptied into an exploitative gaming company's training data without anyone asking, and being mixed into content offered to literal children. For a company being sued by several US states over child safety, "our AI team bulk-downloaded an adult site without looking" is not a good position to be in. If the penalty for a crime is a fine, then that law only exists for the lower class. This section is opinion. Roblox isn't the worst offender in AI's appetite for other people's work, just the latest to turn up in our logs. It isn't the only AI company in them, either. In the month before we found trellis2-data-sourcing , Meta's AI crawler, Meta-ExternalAgent, made about 380,000 requests to our sites, almost all from Meta's own network, and loaded 211,000 project pages. We have since blocked their crawler as well. The Roblox trellis2 crawler is the first individual crawler we spotted that actually pulled assets uploaded by our users, in flagrant defiance of any copyright or license that might apply to it. It fits a broader context, of AI labs taking content without permission. Here's what the largest companies have been accused of, and in some cases have admitted: Meta downloaded at least 81.7 TB of pirated books by torrent from shadow libraries, including through Anna's Archive, according to court filings by the authors suing it. In June 2025 a judge ruled that training on the books was fair use on that record , while stressing that the ruling didn't make Meta's conduct lawful in general. Meta, again: the adult studio Strike 3 Holdings alleges that Meta torrented thousands of its films to train AI video models. Meta says the downloads were for individuals' "personal use". In June 2026 the court refused to dismiss the case . The irony is hard to miss: Strike 3 is best known for suing thousands of individual BitTorrent users. Nvidia contacted Anna's Archive about high-speed access to its collection of pirated books for training data, and management signed off soon after, according to an amended class-action complaint filed in January 2026. Nvidia argued that contacting a pirate site isn't infringement. The court has since largely refused to dismiss the case . Anthropic downloaded hundreds of thousands of pirated books. A judge found that training on books it had bought was fair use, but keeping a library of pirated copies was not. In July 2026 the court approved a $1.5 billion settlement , about $3,000 per book. Now compare how copyright treats everyone else. In the early 2000s Jammie Thomas-Rasset was ordered to pay $222,000 for sharing 24 songs. Internet activist Aaron Swartz faced federal charges carrying decades in prison for downloading academic articles. The Internet Archive, a nonprofit library, lost in court for lending scanned copies of books it owned. Meanwhile, the Internet Archive's online library gets repeatedly scanned by AI companies in return. We'll be honest about where we stand. We don't like copyright as it exists. We'd like to see it radically reformed, and we wouldn't mourn it if it were abolished. Our community lives in its grey areas every day: many of the models on our sites are fan ports of characters from commercial games, made out of love and shared for free. When a studio sends us a takedown notice, we comply. While we as small artists and fan communities get copyright used against us, the world's largest companies are committing copyright infringement at a scale unseen in human history. This has been the case since the invention of the internet of course; digital media make duplication, remixing and resharing trivial, but copyright law never caught up. Filesharing stabbed copyright in the gut. AI is just twisting the knife, and completes the creation an unequal system where copyright infringement is only a crime if you're a low net worth individual. So we aren't asking for stricter copyright laws, or stronger protection for copyright holders. That will only benefit the major entertainment companies like Disney and Adobe who have already stacked the deck in their favor, and are happily making deals with Big-Tech and crushing small creators in the process. We're pointing out that the copyright we have isn't applied equally, and is in practice a two tier system. Individuals face ruinous damages for minor infractions. The largest companies in the world face a cost to be negotiated after the fact, if anyone can afford to sue them. A law that only works downwards gives nobody a reason to respect it, and it can't last in this form. For time being, we'd like to ask Roblox to respect the norms of this community. You credit people. You respect the license they chose. If you want to use someone's work for something they didn't offer it for, you ask. Those norms cost nothing to follow, and Roblox's crawler followed none of them. This scrape attempt saturated the connections for our free download servers for a couple of days, causing problems for our community of legitimate human users. It shows a lack of respect for the people who make this site what it is. those who produced, shared and host the work that you were about to throw in your AI mixer. Questions for Roblox We're sad that the emails we sent to Roblox were not met with a timely response, and would thus like to publicly ask Roblox for its response. These are the questions we'd like Roblox to answer: Did Roblox run the trellis2-data-sourcing crawler? What was the data for? Has any of it been used to train or evaluate a model, and if so, which? Why did the crawler ignore our robots.txt rules and our Terms of Service? Did anyone review which sites the crawler would visit? Was adult content excluded at any stage? Will Roblox delete the files and anything derived from them, and confirm that in writing? Will Roblox respect our creators' license choices, NonCommercial in particular, from now on? We hope Roblox reaches out to us. Also, if you are a person with information on what Roblox is doing, or a fellow site owner who has been targeted, feel free to get in touch as well. We're eager to hear if there's more of a pattern to the scraper's behavior. We've kept the full export of the relevant log files for auditing by external parties if the need arises. About us Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase are three community sites for free 3D resources, run by a small team. SFMLab started in 2014 for Source Filmmaker models. SmutBase followed in 2016 and is exclusively for adult content. Open3DLab, for general-purpose 3D work, joined in 2020. Creators upload characters, props, maps and environments, choose a license for each project, and anyone can download the files for free. All three sites are intended for adults only. About the redaction. The email address in the user agent is a Roblox employee's work address. We've removed the name: this article is about what the Roblox crawler did, not about one person. About Attribution. We take the user agent at face value. Anyone can type any email address into a user agent, and the crawler ran from Amazon's cloud, not from Roblox's own network. Nothing we've seen suggests impersonation, and the label fits Roblox's published research closely. Still, it is a self-description, and it's the first thing we'd like Roblox to confirm. title: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline
body_text: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N.
