Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline 6 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Becca Warner BBC/Serenity Strull (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Birdwatching can help slow brain ageing and is increasingly being used as therapy for dementia patients. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised. Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Blue tits darted between the nearby trees, and Lucy saw Harold laugh for the first time in a long time. "For that moment in time he was present in the moment, he wasn't worried about his memory or his confidence. That is very powerful, in a gentle way," says Jenny Budinger, a community dementia advisor at Age UK, the non-profit that runs the birdwatching group. Birdwatching is increasingly recognised as a valuable way for elderly people and dementia patients to spend their time, with groups set up in nursing homes in the UK, Germany and the US. Paying attention to birds , even through the window, can help older people feel more connected to others, experience more positive emotions and boost memory skills. Now new research shows that birdwatching can reshape the brain, much like learning an athletic sport or a musical instrument – and may even help slow the brain's ageing. Better-organised brains In the laboratory, neuroscientists tested keen birdwatchers' identification skills to determine who was an expert and who was a novice, then looked at their brains. The scientists found that the very structure of experts' brains was different – and that birdwatching expertise might slow age-related decline by keeping the brain more organised. Erik Wing, who led this research at Baycrest Academy for Research and Education in Toronto, Canada, compared MRI brain scans from bird experts to those of novices while they identified birds. He found that expert brains were wired differently in regions important for functions like attention, visual perception and visual recognition. Among expert birders, these regions showed more activity – particularly when they were asked to identify birds they weren't already familiar with. The findings don't prove whether structural brain differences are the cause or effect of birdwatching expertise. But, Wing says, one explanation is that the areas of the brain used for birdwatching might undergo "neuroplasticity" – the ability to change shape and function over time. BBC/Serenity Strull Birdwatching can reshape the brain and may help slow ageing (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Wing also analysed how organised the birdwatchers' brains were. Organisation in the brain tends to reduce with age, and lower measures of organisation are associated with reduced cognition . In experts' brains, some regions had higher levels of organisation and coherence than novices of the same age. Some of these regions were also the ones that showed more activity during bird identification. This indicates a "kind of preservation of organisation" in the brains of experts as they age, Wing says. More research is needed to understand the nature of this preservation and how it links to wider cognitive function. But for now, the results may indicate that "acquiring this skill earlier in life might produce benefits that continue through to older adults", Wing says. This is good news for the many Gen Z (16 to 29-year-old) birdwatchers who are getting their binoculars out long before old age sets in. Bird therapy Wing's research looked at birdwatching expertise, but other findings suggest that there may be psychological benefits to birdwatching even for those without special knowledge or skills. In fact, when it comes to experiencing psychological restoration – feelings of calm, freedom and rejuvenation – enthusiasm may be more relevant than expertise . A study of 388 birdwatchers in Poland found that those who say they are more interested in birding than other activities and consider it an important part of their lives are more likely to experience psychological restoration than birdwatchers who are highly skilled but less enthusiastic. Simply choosing to be interested in birds, then, could have its own benefits. Elisabeth Kals, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt in Germany, is interested in how our relationship with nature shapes our life experiences and wellbeing. She studied what happened when people living in nursing homes had the chance to watch the local bird life. Her team installed bird feeding stations outside 65 homes, positioned so that residents could watch the birds from the comfort of the indoor common area, and assessed the residents' cognition, mobility and wellbeing through self-reports and inputs from staff and family. They saw improvements after just a few weeks, and after a month birdwatching explained residents' wellbeing better than their age and care level. "The findings were clearly positive," Kals says. Those who took part in birdwatching became more cognitively agile, she adds – meaning they were more able to follow a conversation and interact with family who visited, remember and recognise birds that had visited before, and show alertness. Nursing home staff were the first to see the difference the birds made. "For weeks, they haven't seen a smile on [a resident's] face, and then they see the smile," Kals says. Some of the memory and concentration improvements are evident after just three to four weeks, Kals says. Her team's findings have prompted German health insurance companies – who, among others, initially funded the research project – to invest in setting up bird feeders and viewing areas in more than 400 nursing homes across Bavaria. "It was so effective, it just economised money," Kals says. BBC/Serenity Strull Even paying attention to birds through a window can have a positive influence (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) In the US, a similar initiative was set up at four care communities in 2013 in Connecticut, and later in Texas and Colorado . Bird Tales is a therapy programme for people living with dementia that involves installing bird feeders in the facilities where they live and giving them stuffed bird animals that make bird-like calls so they can learn about different species. The result has been positive for those taking part: they report finding it cognitively stimulating and say it connects them with the past. A similar programme has seen benefits for survivors of stroke, some of whom experience aphasia – difficulty speaking or understanding spoken language. The University of Montana's Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Program started with owl spotting in 2021, and now includes guided observations and call identification of Montana's diverse bird population. Why does watching birds have such a positive impact on how we feel and think? For Kals, it's "not just about birds as such; it is about nature, attention, emotion, meaning, social exchange, and activity coming together in a very simple way. It creates small moments of curiosity – pleasure, anticipation". And, she adds, it is "extremely accessible". This may be why, in a UK survey of dementia patients and their carers, watching birds and other wildlife was the second most popular outdoor activity after simply walking in nature. The same survey found that challenges with transport and access are big considerations for people with dementia – which may not be such a barrier for those who can see birds from their kitchen window. Wing says birdwatching is a means of exploring curiosity, and it is perhaps this curiosity that is so beneficial. "I think there's a lot of benefit to incorporating more novelty in our lives, in midlife and as we continue to age," Wing says. Curiosity plays an important role in maintaining cognitive function later in life, possibly because it activates norepinephrine and dopamine in the brain, which have a positive, anti-inflammatory effect. For Kals, getting to know the birds that call and swoop around us is a way to remember who we are. "We are part of nature as human beings, but we lose that connection, unfortunately, quite early in life. [Birdwatching] is a way to reestablish this connection, and it's so simple." * Names have been changed for privacy reasons. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses. A type server maintains the type-analysis state for a workspace and answers requests for the protocol version, snapshots, Python search paths, import resolution, and type queries (computed, declared, and expected types). The protocol uses Language Server Protocol (LSP) data shapes and conventions where they are useful, such as Position and Range , and it represents URIs as strings the same way LSP does. TSP methods use the typeServer/ prefix. The protocol artifacts in this folder are the authoritative definitions: typeServerProtocol.ts defines the TypeScript interfaces and request types. tsp.json is the machine-readable protocol model. tsp.schema.json is the JSON schema for the protocol model. Version History TSP uses semantic version strings for client/server compatibility checks. While the protocol is in the 0.x line, minor version changes may be breaking. Patch version changes remain backward compatible within the same minor line. Version Changes 0.1.0 Initial protocol version. 0.2.0 Added request types and fields. 0.3.0 Switched to more complex type shapes. 0.4.0 Switched to the Type union and stub-based type payloads. 0.4.1 Added multi-connection negotiation and the typeServer/connection control request. Connection Model A client starts a type server and communicates with it over the main JSON-RPC connection using a transport the server supports, such as stdio or Node IPC. When using stdio, stdout must be reserved for JSON-RPC protocol messages. A type server is expected to receive enough workspace and document state to answer the TSP requests it supports. Clients commonly use normal LSP initialization and document synchronization for this state, then send typeServer/* requests on the same JSON-RPC connection. TSP also supports optional extra read-only connections. The original connection remains the main connection and owns initialization, workspace state, document synchronization, state-changing notifications, and connection control. Extra connections are opened only after client and server negotiate support during initialization. Startup Sequence A typical session follows this order: The client starts or connects to the type server. The client and server initialize any shared workspace state, commonly through the LSP initialize and initialized messages. The client calls typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion and verifies that the returned semver string is compatible with the protocol version it expects. The client calls typeServer/getSnapshot to obtain the first snapshot identifier. The client sends type-query, import-resolution, or search-path requests that include the current snapshot when required by the request shape. The server sends typeServer/snapshotChanged when prior type results are no longer valid. Multi-Connection Mode Multi-connection mode is an optional performance feature. It lets a client open additional local channels to the same type server for read-only TSP requests, while the main connection continues to own the mutable workspace state. Clients should use multi-connection mode only when they can benefit from concurrent read-only work, such as high-volume type queries or background workers that should not block the main JSON-RPC connection. A server must still work correctly in single-connection mode. Multi-connection support must not be required for protocol correctness. Capability Handshake Multi-connection support is negotiated through the normal LSP initialize request and response. A client that can open extra TSP channels advertises the supported transport kinds under capabilities.experimental.typeServerMultiConnection : { "capabilities" : { "experimental" : { "typeServerMultiConnection" : { "supportedTransports" : [ " ipc " ] } } } } A server that can serve extra TSP channels returns the same capability shape in the initialize result: { "capabilities" : { "experimental" : { "typeServerMultiConnection" : { "supportedTransports" : [ " ipc " ] } } } } Multi-connection mode is enabled only when both sides advertise typeServerMultiConnection and the two supportedTransports lists have at least one transport in common. If either side omits the capability, or if there is no common transport, the session remains single-connection and the client must not send typeServer/connection . The currently supported built-in transport kind for extra connections is ipc . This negotiation is separate from the main connection, which can use stdio or Node IPC. Opening An Extra Connection After initialization and transport negotiation, the client opens an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection: { "type" : " open " , "kind" : " ipc " , "args" : [ " <ipc-endpoint> " ] } For ipc , the args array identifies the endpoint or endpoints that the server should connect to. The server should validate the request, connect to the supplied endpoint promptly, and return a result with success: true when it accepts the request. If the server cannot open the channel, it should return success: false and include a short message when useful for logs. IPC Endpoint Arguments An ipc endpoint is expected to provide a full-duplex JSON-RPC stream when the platform IPC mechanism supports it. In that case, args contains one endpoint string: { "type" : " open " , "kind" : " ipc " , "args" : [ " <full-duplex-ipc-endpoint> " ] } If the platform IPC mechanism exposes only one-way endpoints, args contains two endpoint strings. The endpoint names are from the type server's perspective: the first endpoint is the server input stream, and the second endpoint is the server output stream. { "type" : " open " , "kind" : " ipc " , "args" : [ " <input-ipc-endpoint> " , " <output-ipc-endpoint> " ] } Closing An Extra Connection The client closes an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection with the same transport kind and endpoint identity: { "type" : " close " , "kind" : " ipc " , "args" : [ " <ipc-endpoint> " ] } The server should stop serving the matching extra channel and close the transport promptly. A client may also tear down its local transport if the server does not complete the close within the client's timeout budget. The close request should use the same args shape that opened the channel: one endpoint for a full-duplex IPC stream, or the same input/output endpoint pair for a split IPC stream. Allowed Traffic The main connection owns all state-changing traffic. The following must remain main-connection-only: LSP initialization and lifecycle messages. Workspace, configuration, file-watcher, and document synchronization notifications. Server-to-client snapshot notifications. The typeServer/connection control request. Extra connections are TSP-only and read-only. They may be used for requests that do not mutate server state and whose results are valid for the snapshot supplied by the client. The allowed TSP messages on an extra connection are bound to the negotiated TSP version. If a server reports support for a TSP version and advertises multi-connection support for that session, it must support every extra-connection TSP message defined for that version. The table below lists the TSP version that first allows each message on an extra connection: TSP version Extra-connection message 0.4.1 typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion 0.4.1 typeServer/getSnapshot 0.4.1 typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths 0.4.1 typeServer/resolveImport 0.4.1 typeServer/getComputedType 0.4.1 typeServer/getDeclaredType 0.4.1 typeServer/getExpectedType Servers should reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection , and any TSP message not allowed for the negotiated TSP version when received on an extra connection. Snapshots A snapshot is a non-negative integer that identifies a point-in-time view of the type server's analysis state. Type handles, declarations, symbols, and other returned objects are valid only for the snapshot in which they were returned unless a request explicitly says otherwise. The type server must advance the snapshot whenever a previously returned type-analysis result may be invalid. Typical invalidating events include opened-file changes, closed files, configuration changes, watched-file changes, dependency changes, or any cache reset that changes analysis results. Snapshot rules: typeServer/getSnapshot returns the current snapshot identifier. Snapshot identifiers must not decrease during a session. typeServer/snapshotChanged reports the previous and new snapshot identifiers. Requests that include a stale snapshot should fail with a JSON-RPC error that lets the client retry with a fresh snapshot. LSP's ServerCancelled error code ( -32802 ) is the preferred error for this case. Positions And Ranges TSP follows LSP position conventions: Lines are zero-based. Character offsets are zero-based UTF-16 code units. Ranges identify source spans using a start position and end position. If a type server stores source locations in another encoding, it must convert locations at the protocol boundary. Incorrect conversion can cause the client to request information for the wrong syntax node. Nodes, Declarations, And Handles The type-query requests ( typeServer/getComputedType , typeServer/getDeclaredType , typeServer/getExpectedType ) identify a source construct with an arg that is either a node or a declaration. A node is a URI plus a source range. A declaration describes where and how a symbol is defined and is either a regular declaration, which is backed by a source AST node, or a synthesized declaration, which is created by the type checker and has no source node. InvalidHandle is -1 and represents an invalid or unavailable handle. Clients and servers should treat it as a sentinel value, not as a valid object identifier. Type Results Type results are JSON-serializable tagged objects. Each type includes a discriminator that tells the client how to interpret the rest of the object. The protocol supports built-in types, declared types, functions, classes, unions, modules, type variables, overload sets, synthesized types, and type references. Every type object carries a numeric kind discriminator, a numeric id , and a bitfield of flags : kind Type Description 0 BuiltIn unknown , any , unbound , ellipsis , never , and similar 1 Declared Base for source-declared types (rarely used directly) 2 Function Functions and methods from def statements 3 Class Classes and their instances 4 Union Union types ( int | str | None ) 5 Module Module objects ( import os produces a Module type for os ) 6 TypeVar Type variables ( T , P , Ts ) 7 Overloaded Functions with multiple @overload signatures 8 Synthesized Types synthesized by the type checker 9 TypeReference Reference to another type by id , used for deduplication and cycles Type objects are snapshot-bound, and type IDs are response-local: A returned type object is valid only for the snapshot used by the request that produced it. Type IDs are used to connect TypeReference objects to earlier type objects in the same serialized response graph. Type IDs are not a stable global identity for a snapshot and should not be compared across separate responses. Type references should be used to avoid duplicating large or recursive type graphs within one response. Protocol Surface The current protocol is intentionally small. The exact parameters and result shapes are defined in the protocol artifacts; the table below lists every TSP message with its direction and payload shape. Message Direction Params Result typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion client → server none string (semver) typeServer/getSnapshot client → server none number typeServer/snapshotChanged server → client { old: number, new: number } notification typeServer/connection client → server { type: "open" | "close", kind, args? } { success, message? } typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths client → server { fromUri, snapshot } string[] | undefined typeServer/resolveImport client → server { sourceUri, moduleDescriptor, snapshot } string | undefined typeServer/getComputedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined typeServer/getDeclaredType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined typeServer/getExpectedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined A type server should implement the messages required by the client it integrates with and return undefined only where the protocol's result type allows it. Type Queries The three type-query requests differ by which type they report for the same node or declaration: typeServer/getComputedType returns the type inferred from code flow. After narrowing a to int , the computed type of b in b = a + 1 is int . typeServer/getDeclaredType returns the type explicitly written in the source. For def foo(a: int | str) , the declared type of a is int | str . typeServer/getExpectedType returns the type the surrounding context expects. For the call foo(4) , the expected type of the argument is int | str . Error Handling Use standard JSON-RPC error responses. Situation Error code Guidance Stale snapshot -32802 ( ServerCancelled ) The client can request a fresh snapshot and retry. Invalid parameters -32602 ( InvalidParams ) Required fields are missing or malformed. Internal failure -32603 ( InternalError ) The server failed unexpectedly while handling a valid request. Errors should include enough message detail for a client log to identify the failed request, but they should not expose local secrets or implementation-only state. Compatibility Checklist A compatible type server should verify these behaviors: typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion returns a semver string supported by the client. All request and notification payloads serialize and deserialize according to the protocol artifacts. typeServer/getSnapshot returns a non-negative snapshot and snapshots do not go backward. Document, configuration, and watched-file changes invalidate snapshots when they can change returned analysis data. Requests with stale snapshots fail with a retryable cancellation error. Position and range conversions use LSP zero-based UTF-16 conventions. Import-resolution requests return document URIs or no result according to the protocol result type. Type queries (computed, declared, and expected) return well-formed Type objects, or undefined , for the snapshot supplied by the client. Multi-connection support is advertised only when the server can serve the negotiated extra transport. Extra connections accept every TSP request allowed for the negotiated TSP version and reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection , and TSP requests not allowed for that version. title: New iPad mini
body_text: Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever - Apple Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + Newsroom Open Newsroom navigation Close Newsroom navigation Apple Services Apple Stories Search Newsroom Close opens in new window PRESS RELEASE October 26, 2026 Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever Featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance, faster wireless connectivity, and water and dust resistance The new iPad mini offers the full iPad experience users can hold in the palm of their hand. CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today unveiled the all-new iPad mini , featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. 1 The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. 2 A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. 3 With its incredible set of advanced features, it’s the most capable and versatile iPad mini ever. The new iPad mini is powered by iPadOS 27 with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions on virtually any topic with broad world knowledge, and understand what’s on their screen. 4 The combination of powerful features and game-changing iPadOS 27 capabilities makes the new iPad mini a compelling value. Customers can pre-order it along with the new Smart Folio starting Wednesday, October 28, with availability beginning Friday, November 6. “iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.” iPad mini is beloved by creators, small business owners, doctors, field service workers, gamers, and more, for its portability, performance, and display. Thinner and Lighter Than Ever At 5.4 mm thin, the new iPad mini is more portable than ever, and is available in two gorgeous finishes: a new midnight and a beautiful starlight. Remarkably thinner and lighter than the previous generation, iPad mini is now even easier to carry, whether a user is reading, working on the go, or using it with one hand. It also features an IP67 rating to protect against water and dust — ideal for a range of use cases, such as working outside on a rainy day or reading by the pool. 1 iPad mini is shown in midnight. iPad mini is shown in starlight. iPad mini is shown lying flat with droplets of water on it. The new iPad mini comes in two gorgeous finishes, including a new midnight. The new iPad mini comes in two gorgeous finishes, including the beautiful starlight. iPad mini now has an IP67 rating to protect against water and dust. previous next A Stunning OLED Display The new iPad mini comes with a stunning OLED display that delivers amazing front-of-screen performance and an even larger 8.5-inch size while maintaining the same footprint as the previous mini, thanks to 24 percent thinner bezels. 2 The Super Retina XDR display features OLED technology to deliver pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate imagery. The Super Retina XDR display features OLED technology that delivers amazing front-of-screen performance. For an even better visual experience across a range of lighting conditions, iPad mini also features peak brightness of up to 1200 nits — more than 2x higher than the previous generation — and supports 600 nits of full-screen brightness for SDR and HDR content, along with a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. And with a 1-nit minimum brightness, iPad mini is even more suitable for dim environments, from users reading in bed at night to pilots checking their electronic flight bag in the cockpit. iPad mini also offers a new nano-texture display option, which users love on iPad Pro, that reduces glare in bright environments — ideal for creatives editing outdoors or technicians working in the field. Together, these display advancements extend the versatility of iPad mini across an even wider range of use cases. iPad mini offers a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare in bright environments. A Huge Leap in Performance A20 Pro delivers a giant leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. It is built using Apple’s latest 2-nanometer process technology and a new package inspired by M-series chips. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, iPad mini delivers up to 4.5x faster AI performance than the previous generation — perfect for AI tasks ranging from running on-device models in creative apps to running local LLMs. 3 And with the latest graphics architecture, including dynamic caching and hardware-accelerated mesh shading and ray tracing, graphics performance jumps by up to 2.7x — great for gaming and 3D rendering. 3 A20 Pro also features up to a 6-core CPU for up to 60 percent faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks like editing photos and working across apps. 3 A20 Pro delivers a huge leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. The 512GB configuration features a powerful Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which offers double the processing power of the previous generation, accelerating tasks in apps like Draw Things and Detail. By engaging all 32 cores, A20 Pro becomes a powerhouse for more advanced on-device AI workloads. A20 Pro also brings over a 2x increase in unified memory bandwidth, unlocking additional performance for new levels of capability and responsiveness across graphics and AI-intensive workloads. With a faster CPU and GPU, as well as an increase in unified memory, working in apps like Procreate Dreams is faster than ever. A Rich New Audio Experience and Advanced Cameras The new iPad mini features an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume. In addition, custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs. The Acoustic Display also features a sealed enclosure that helps iPad mini achieve its IP67 rating. The 12MP Center Stage front camera is now on the landscape edge, perfect for FaceTime calls, video conferencing, and collaboration. And the 12MP Wide back camera captures gorgeous photos with Smart HDR 4 and 4K video at up to 60 fps, while the addition of an Adaptive True Tone flash improves photos and makes document scanning better than ever. FaceTime calls, video conferencing, and collaboration feel more natural than ever with the 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge. N1 and C2 Come to iPad mini iPad mini now features N1, an Apple-designed wireless networking chip that enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. 5 N1 brings better performance when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the overall performance and reliability of features like AirDrop and AirPlay. 6 Cellular models of the new iPad mini feature C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system. C2 enables up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds compared to the previous generation of iPad mini, with even greater power efficiency. 6 And with iPadOS 27, moving between cellular and Wi-Fi networks is more seamless than ever, so users can stay connected on a FaceTime call even while they’re in transit. Users can also enjoy the benefits of eSIM, which lets them quickly and securely add a new plan, connect and transfer existing plans digitally, and stay in touch with family and friends regardless of Wi-Fi availability. 7 The N1 wireless networking chip and C2 modem come to iPad mini for the first time, enabling faster connectivity. iPadOS 27 with the Next Generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI iPad mini users can get even more done with Siri AI, rolling out in beta with iPadOS 27. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri, powered by Apple Intelligence, that is profoundly more personal, capable, and conversational. 4 iPad mini also supports Apple’s most advanced on-device model ever, for even more expressive voices with Siri AI as well as a major boost in accuracy with systemwide dictation. The next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI helps users get even more done. Siri AI can draw on personal context understanding to help users find what they need in the moment across their personal messages, emails, photos, and more; use onscreen awareness to take action related to the content on a user’s screen; and answer questions about virtually any topic. Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. Users can improve a photo’s composition after it’s been taken using tools such as upgraded Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, and Extend. And now the all-new Image Playground app offers photorealistic imagery. In Safari, Notify Me helps users monitor web pages for changes, like product restocks or price drops, and stay on top of updates. Apple Intelligence uses on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute to help protect users’ privacy. When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else. iPadOS 27 also delivers an expansive set of improvements that make iPad more responsive, reliable, and easy to use, along with updates to Liquid Glass, including a new slider in Settings that gives users the option to personalize it, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference. With iPadOS 27.2, iPad mini also supports extended display mode when connected to an external display, great for users multitasking with windowed apps. With iPadOS 27, users can enhance their productivity and creativity by multitasking with freely resizable windows, window tiling, and Exposé. Additionally, powerful and easy-to-use tools help parents manage what their kids can see, who they can talk to, and when they have access to apps. For parents and families looking for more information on how to help create safer, more enriching digital experiences for their kids, Apple also has a website with details on the latest tools and how to get started using them. Accessories That Unlock More Ways to Be Productive and Creative The new Smart Folio features a two-panel architecture, offering a slim, lightweight cover that magnetically attaches to iPad mini. 8 Crafted with TechWoven fabric in navy blue and taupe to complement the iPad mini finishes, the Smart Folio has an adjustable design that gives users a greater range of motion, including new viewing angles, for enhanced versatility. Crafted with TechWoven fabric in navy blue and taupe, the new Smart Folio features a two-panel architecture, offering a slim, lightweight cover for iPad mini. iPad mini supports both Apple Pencil (USB-C) and Apple Pencil Pro, giving users two incredible options to bring their ideas to life. 8 Apple Pencil (USB-C) is a great value for everyday tasks like note-taking and sketching, while Apple Pencil Pro delivers industry-leading capabilities for the ultimate pencil experience. With Apple Pencil Pro, users can take advantage of innovative features like squeeze and barrel roll to work in entirely new ways, as well as utilize Find My support to help locate it when misplaced. With advanced features like squeeze and barrel roll, Apple Pencil Pro makes creating in apps like Procreate more intuitive than ever. iPad mini and the Environment iPad mini was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 35 percent recycled content overall, 9 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure and 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery. iPad mini is manufactured with 40 percent renewable energy, like wind and solar, across the supply chain. It is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled. Pricing and Availability Customers can pre-order iPad mini with A20 Pro starting Wednesday, October 28, at apple.com and in the Apple Store app in 36 countries and regions, including the U.S. It will begin arriving to customers, and will be in Apple Store locations and Apple Authorized Resellers, starting Friday, November 6. iPad mini will be available in midnight and starlight with 128GB, 256GB, and 512GB configurations. iPad mini starts at $699 (U.S.) or $58.25 (U.S.) per month for 12 months for the Wi-Fi model, and $849 (U.S.) or $70.75 (U.S.) per month for 12 months for the Wi-Fi + Cellular model. 11 Apple Upgrade leasing prices for the iPad mini start at $14.99 (U.S.) per month for a 36-month lease for the Wi-Fi model, and $18.21 (U.S.) per month for a 36-month lease for the Wi-Fi + Cellular model. 12 With education savings, iPad mini starts at $649 (U.S.) or $54.08 (U.S.) per month for 12 months. 11 The new TechWoven Smart Folio is available in navy blue and taupe, and is available for $79 (U.S.). Apple Pencil Pro and Apple Pencil (USB-C) are compatible with the new iPad mini. Apple Pencil Pro is available for $129 (U.S.) and $119 (U.S.) with education savings. Apple Pencil (USB-C) is available for $79 (U.S.) and $69 (U.S.) with education savings. AppleCare delivers exceptional service and support, with flexible options for Apple users. Customers can choose AppleCare+ to cover their new iPad or, in available markets, AppleCare One to protect multiple products in one simple plan. Both plans include coverage for accidents like drops and spills, theft and loss protection on eligible products, battery replacement service, and priority support from Apple Experts. In the U.S., customers can also choose AppleCare One Family, which extends that same coverage to every eligible device across an Apple Family Sharing group for one fixed monthly price. For more information, visit apple.com/applecare . Apple offers great ways to save on the latest iPad. Customers can trade in their current iPad and get credit toward a new one by visiting the Apple Store online, the Apple Store app, or an Apple Store location. To see what their device is worth, and for terms and conditions, customers can visit apple.com/shop/trade-in . 13 Customers in the U.S. who shop at Apple using Apple Card 14 can pay monthly at 0 percent APR when they choose to check out with Apple Card Monthly Installments, 15 and they’ll get 3 percent Daily Cash back — all up front. More information — including details on eligibility, exclusions, and Apple Card terms — is available at apple.com/apple-card/monthly-installments . Customers in the U.S. can also pay for their Wi-Fi + Cellular iPad mini over time when they choose to finance with a carrier. title: Websites Should Be Printable
body_text: Websites Should Be Printable Brennen Puth Home Projects Contact Websites Should Be Printable 2026-10-24 I'm looking for work! (click to expand) If you have questions or thoughts on the post I'd love to hear about it! I'm currently looking for work in the northeastern US. I'll be graduating with a BS in both Computer Science and Cyber Operations at the end of the school year. I have worked in web application development and Java, and I have experience in Rust, C++, Python, and various other languages. If you're curious about what I've done in the past, I keep up a short list of projects here or contact me to give me a place to send my resume. I figure anyone who reads my posts will have an interesting offer, so all leads are appreciated! I read a lot of printed papers these days. While I enjoy reading on a laptop as much as the next guy, marking up a printed document engages me better. Also, there's something about sitting with a whiteboard and a printed document that makes me rightly feel like I'm doing something important. So I've been thinking about how to best allow others to enjoy this medium for content that I write. Luckily for me, printed documents were a major focus of web design a while ago. You can print any webpage you like, by hitting CTRL-P and hoping your printer driver decides to cooperate today. I tested this on my own webpage, foolishly thinking I would have a decent print job without any effort. It wasn't great, although you can at least see all the content. The text was too big by about 2 levels, the header looks awful when printed, and my links look awfully gray in black-and-white. Totally unacceptable. Making Things Printable Edit 2026-10-26: I feel it's relevant to say, this has almost entirely changed already because of feedback I received from people both on lobste.rs and HN about obvious things I'd missed. I'm currently simplifying my stylesheet as much as I can. Thanks! Luckily, the web community has had this aforementioned focus on printing documents from HTML pages. CSS has selectors to allow styling specifically printed content, and they can be useful. Here's my print-related snippet for this page now: . onlyPrint { display : none ; } @media print { . noPrint { display : none ; } . onlyPrint { display : inline ; } p , ol { font-size : 12 pt ; } h3 , h4 { font-size : 13 pt ; } h2 { font-size : 14 pt ; } h1 { font-size : 16 pt ; } . giallo { border : 3 px solid black ; } . giallo-l { font-size : 11 pt ; } a { color : black !important ; } } You can see the effects of this snippet by hitting CTRL-P or the print button on this page. Here's the functions this does for me, in order: onlyPrint can be added as a class to allow elements which only show up in the printed document. Right now, that means tagging a small author attribution to the subtitle. noPrint is used to remove something from the printed website. I put it on the header, because it looks honestly very ugly in printed format. Adjusting font sizes for print is very important. The variable-scale text which I use on my website looks awful on a printed page. 12pt is a fairly well accepted size, so I figured it'll do. A slightly larger size for the headers makes sense as well. The giallo tweaks are for codeblocks. Honestly, codeblocks are still the ugliest part even after some tweaking. They want to come out as one chunk and not break over page borders, and if anyone has a solution to that I'd be greatly appreciative. Blue links, as much as I like them on the site, look awful in grayscale. Turning them the same color as other text is fine. Feel free to pull any code you like from the CSS, I'm not protective of it. I would personally love to experience more webpages that think about how printing works. Why You Should Do This After attempting to optimize my website in this way, I am sympathetic for those who wouldn't prioritize printing. Hiding and showing all the right things in print took me a decent chunk of my morning. My site isn't very complex. I also doubt how many people regularly print webpages out. I might be the only one. Still, if all your website consists of is text, allowing people to experience the text in their favorite medium is never a bad thing. The digital medium allows a lot of flexibility. The road to good software is paved with kindnesses from software engineers to their users. One day, perhaps someone shall find this kindness and smile, even if just for a fleeting moment. And that will be worth it. Edit 2026-10-26: I was informed by a friend that this post ended up on the front page of HN and lobste.rs after I submitted it. Fun! Despite the several flaws I am now informed of in my CSS, I hope this article at least pushes a few to consider this medium more carefully. Thanks all for reading!

PaperPilot PDF tools for your AI agent — and for you. Pure Rust. Runs locally. Files never leave your machine. Try it in your browser → · Download · Contributing · Roadmap PaperPilot is a PDF and document toolkit written in Rust. The same engine runs as: Surface Use it for MCP server Give Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, Pi, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP client the ability to merge, split, OCR, and compress PDFs CLI Batch and scripted workflows Browser (WASM) Zero-install tools; files are processed in browser memory, nothing is uploaded Desktop app Tauri + Svelte GUI with viewer, markup, and diff Local REST API Call it from Python, Node, or n8n at localhost:7823 No Chromium, no C++ runtime, no cloud calls. Open-WebUI integration (source builds): use the local gateway as a PDF-only Tika-compatible extraction server. See the Open-WebUI setup guide . Quick start 1. Use it with your coding agent (MCP) Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, and current Pi releases connect to the same local stdio server. See the coding agent setup guide for each client's configuration and verification steps. Builds from this source can also print ready-to-merge configuration: paperpilot-mcp --client-config codex # Also: claude-code, kimi-code, pi, claude-desktop, cursor Download paperpilot-mcp from Releases , then add it to claude_desktop_config.json : { "mcpServers" : { "paperpilot" : { "command" : " /path/to/paperpilot-mcp " } } } Restart Claude and try: "Merge these two PDFs and compress the result." 2. Use the CLI # Merge paperpilot merge --inputs doc1.pdf doc2.pdf --output merged.pdf # Compress paperpilot compress --input in.pdf --quality 75 --output compressed.pdf # Rotate pages 1, 3–5 by 90° paperpilot rotate --input in.pdf --pages 1,3-5 --angle 90 --output out.pdf 3. Use it in the browser Go to usepaperpilot.com . Open your browser's Network tab while you work — you'll see no file uploads. 4. Build from source git clone https://github.com/KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot.git cd PaperPilot cargo build --release -p paperpilot-cli -p paperpilot-mcp -p paperpilot-gateway Desktop app: cd apps/desktop && pnpm install && pnpm tauri dev Requires Rust 1.75+, Node.js, and pnpm. What it can do today (v0.6) Organize & Layout: merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages, extract pages, booklet imposition, N-up grid, multi-sheet poster tile slicing ( pdf_posterize ) Optimize & Compress: lossy compression, stream deduplication, CMYK safety guards Extract & Ingest: structured text, detected Markdown tables, native Open-WebUI & Apache Tika ingestion adapter ( /tika/text , /tika/json/md , /rmeta/text ), pure-Rust OCR (PaddleOCR via rten ) Security & Analysis: watermark, validate signatures, remove signatures, PII scan, deep sanitize, malformed fuzzing & panic-free error handling Office Data: Excel → JSON, Excel → CSV Why another PDF tool? Private by default. Everything runs locally or in your browser tab. Agent-ready. MCP support is first-class, not an afterthought. One engine, many surfaces. CLI, MCP, REST, WASM, and desktop share the same Rust core, so behavior is consistent. Small and dependency-light. Pure Rust, built on lopdf , pdf_oxide , rten , and friends. Benchmarks Run cargo bench --workspace to reproduce. Methodology and results: SYSTEM_BENCHMARK_REPORT.md . Architecture Desktop (Tauri) · CLI · REST (Axum) · MCP (stdio) · WASM (browser / edge) │ Rust core workspace paperpilot-core · paperpilot-pdf · paperpilot-nlp · paperpilot-gateway paperpilot-mcp · paperpilot-wasm · paperpilot-storage Embed in your own site < script src =" https://cdn.usepaperpilot.com/embed.js " data-tools =" merge,compress,ocr " > </ script > < div id =" paperpilot-widget " > </ div > Local REST API & Document Ingestion paperpilot serve --port 7823 # Standard PDF Operations (JSON & multipart) curl -X POST http://localhost:7823/api/v1/pdf/merge \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"inputs": ["a.pdf", "b.pdf"], "output": "out.pdf"} ' # Open-WebUI & Tika In-Memory Ingestion (sub-5ms) curl -X PUT http://localhost:7823/tika/text \ -H " Content-Type: application/pdf " \ --data-binary @sample.pdf Interactive Swagger OpenAPI docs at http://localhost:7823/swagger-ui . Contributing & Community Issues and PRs are welcome. Good first contributions: bug reports with a sample PDF, new tool requests, and docs fixes. Special thanks to all community members and contributors recognized in CONTRIBUTORS.md . License Community Edition (this repo): Apache 2.0 . It includes the CLI, MCP server, REST gateway, WASM engine, and desktop app. An Enterprise Edition (SSO, RBAC, audit logs, DLP) is developed separately. August 18, 2026 Table of contents This article is about our commercial products such as Claude for Work and the Anthropic API. For our consumer products such as Claude Free, Pro, Max and when accounts from those plans use Claude Code, see here . By default, we will not use your inputs or outputs from our commercial products (e.g. Claude for Work, Anthropic API, Claude Gov, etc.) to train our models. If you explicitly report feedback or bugs to us (e.g. via our thumbs up/down feedback button), or otherwise choose to allow us to use your data, then we may use your chats and coding sessions to train our models. To find out more information regarding your use of an Anthropic commercial offering, or if you would like to know how to contact us regarding a privacy related topic, see our Trust Center and Commercial Terms . Feedback When you provide us feedback via our thumbs up / down button, we will store the entire related conversation, including any content, custom styles, conversation preferences, or model settings, in our secured back-end for up to 5 years. Feedback data does not include raw content from connectors (e.g. Google Drive), including remote and local MCP servers, though data may be included if it’s directly copied into your conversation with Claude. We de-link your feedback from your user and customer IDs before it’s used by Anthropic. We may use your feedback to analyze the effectiveness of our services, conduct research, study user behavior, and train our AI models as permitted under applicable laws. We do not combine your feedback with your other conversations with Claude. Inspired by her father’s inability to read and write Dolly started her Imagination Library in 1995 for the children within her home county. Today, her program spans five countries and gifts millions of free books each month to children around the world. “When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer. The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.” In 1995, Dolly Parton launched an exciting new effort,  Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , to benefit the children of her home county in East Tennessee, USA. Dolly’s vision was to foster a love of reading among her county’s preschool children and their families by providing them with the gift of a specially selected book each month. title: Growing Trees
body_text: Chema Guerra Archive About Growing trees Oct 15, 2026 • Chema Guerra A procedurally grown linden. The branching structure comes from the simulation described below. I’ve been playing with procedural tree growth recently. The method I am using is based on Self-organizing tree models for image synthesis , by Palubicki et al. (SIGGRAPH 2009). The idea is beautifully simple: buds compete for light, the tree distributes a growth resource among them, and the successful ones produce new shoots. Those shoots change the light available for the next round. The crown shape emerges from this feedback loop. Here is a quick breakdown, with some visualizations from my implementation. One season at a time The basic building block is a metamer : an internode (a short piece of stem), a leaf, and the buds at its upper node. A terminal bud continues an axis, and axillary buds may start lateral branches. Each iteration represents one growing season: Measure the light available to every bud. Sum that light from the tips down to the root. Distribute a proportional growth resource back up the tree. Grow shoots from the buds that receive enough resource. Shed poorly lit branches and age dormant buds. The same seed growing from season 2 through 30. The camera and scale stay fixed. Where is the light? One way to approximate light availability is a voxel grid. Each bud adds shadow to a widening pyramid of voxels below it, with its contribution decaying with depth. Contributions from all buds add up, so the interior naturally becomes darker as the tree grows. Each bud reads two things from this grid: an available-light value \(Q\), and a direction \(\mathbf{V}\) toward the least shaded neighboring voxel inside its perception cone. Left: a vertical slice through the shadow grid. Right: light per bud. Cyan buds are well exposed. Orange ones are shaded. The paper also supports space colonization : fill an envelope with marker points, let buds compete for nearby markers, and remove markers as growth occupies their space. Same growth machinery, a different way to decide where growth is possible. Who gets to grow? Light values are first summed down the branching structure. At the base, the total \(Q_{base}\) becomes a growth resource \(v=\alpha Q_{base}\). This resource travels back up, splitting at every branching point. Left: accumulated light flowing down. Right: resource flowing up. Orange dots mark buds that receive enough to grow. In the extended Borchert-Honda model, the main continuation receives: \[v_m=v\frac{\lambda Q_m}{\lambda Q_m+(1-\lambda)Q_l}\] The lateral side receives the remainder. At \(\lambda=0.5\), resource follows light. Larger values favor the main axis. Smaller values favor the laterals. This little bias has a surprisingly large effect: Left: lambda=0.46, a spreading crown. Right: lambda=0.56, a dominant leader. A bud receiving less than one unit stays dormant. Otherwise it produces a shoot of \(\lfloor v\rfloor\) metamers, subject to a configured cap. New metamers receive their own buds, and the process repeats. Magic! Which way? Each new segment follows a normalized weighted sum of its previous direction, the light-seeking direction \(\mathbf{V}\), an upward or downward tropism , and some noise. A horizontal component can make lateral branches spread into flat tiers. Bud placement around the stem ( phyllotaxis ) provides another important control. Spiral arrangements, opposite pairs, and annual whorls produce very different branching patterns. The frame is parallel-transported along the shoot so the arrangement stays coherent as it bends. Six phyllotaxis patterns, seen down the shoot axis. Numbers identify consecutive nodes. Dropping branches and adding girth With the shadow model, a lateral branch is shed when the light collected by its subtree, divided by its metamer count, falls below a threshold. Young branches get a grace period. Otherwise the inner crown would keep accumulating starved twigs. Same seed, without shedding (left) and with it (right). Self-pruning changes the light available for subsequent growth too. Branch thickness comes afterwards, using a pipe model : \[r_{parent}^{n}=\sum_i r_i^{n}\] Start with a fixed radius at the tips and accumulate toward the root. For \(n=2\), cross-sectional area is preserved at junctions. Larger exponents produce slenderer trunks. Shed branches still contribute to the girth below them. Losing a branch does not make the trunk shrink. Width and passive sag are calculated from the grown skeleton and do not feed back into growth. From branches to foliage The skeleton becomes a bark mesh by sweeping tubes along its axes. For foliage I use twig spray cards : each card depicts a small twig carrying several leaves, using variants from a procedurally drawn atlas. The twig atlas and the cards that carry it. Each card replaces a whole clump of leaves. Blending the card normals toward an ellipsoid around the crown helps the foliage shade as a volume. Lower detail levels retain fewer, larger cards and simplify the bark. At a distance, baked directional impostors take over. Bonus: The grown tree can also be baked into depth-field views for forest rendering. The image below uses many instances of one baked linden, with size variation. The forest representation and lighting deserve a separate post, though. One grown tree, instanced as a forest using baked depth-field views. Chema Guerra brashandplucky@gmail.com @chemaguerra @topotoylabs This is a coding blog where I post about the various projects that I am currently working on, both at work, or as an independent researcher. Most content here revolves around computer graphics and physics simulation.

body_text: Pharo - Pharo 14 Released! Toggle navigation News Features Download Documentation Community Contribute Stories About Download latest version ($.0) Learn more --> Pharo 14 Released! Dear Pharo users and dynamic language lovers: We have released Pharo version 14! What is Pharo? Pharo is a pure object-oriented programming language and a powerful environment focused on simplicity and immediate feedback. Screenshot of Pharo 14 Simple & powerful language: No constructors, no types declaration, no interfaces, no primitive types. Yet a powerful and elegant language with a full syntax fitting in one postcard! Pharo is objects and messages all the way down. Live, immersive environment: Immediate feedback at any moment of your development: Developing, testing, debugging. Even in production environments, you will never be stuck in compiling and deploying steps again! Amazing debugging experience: Pharo environment includes a debugger unlike anything you've seen before. It allows you to step through code, restart the execution of methods, create methods on the fly, and much more! Pharo is yours: Pharo is made by an incredible community, with more than [X] contributors for the last revision of the platform and hundreds of people constantly contributing with frameworks and libraries. Fully open-source: Pharo full stack is released under MIT License and available on GitHub ... more on the Pharo Features page . In this iteration of Pharo, our efforts have concentrated on three main areas: Modernizing the development tools. We introduced Mission Control and Pulse (the replacement for Spotter), reworked the Method Browser and rewrote the Settings Browser, and consolidated Epicea and ProfStef into NewTools. This continues our ongoing migration of the development tools to the Spec-based tooling stack. Rebuilding the refactoring and command infrastructure. Refactoring commands were migrated to a driver-based architecture behind a unified command registry, and we kept expanding Pharo's command-line capabilities (command-line testing, a command-line debugger, and Sindarin script tooling). Modernizing the virtual machine. We unified frames and stack management, added RISC-V JIT support, extended memory management (direct old-space allocation and GC improvements), advanced Slang/C compilation, and modernized the cross-platform build infrastructure. Worth noting: starting with this release, we have moved our release schedule from spring (MarchâMay) to fall (SeptemberâNovember). Pharo 14 is the first version released under the new schedule. Some highlights of this amazing version: Highlights Tools Introduction of Mission Control New/reworked Method Browser Settings Browser rewrite and switch to default Epicea migration into NewTools ProfStef migration into NewTools Introduction of Pulse (Spotter replacement) TestRunner integration and command-line testing Calypso fixes Cavrois / window profile work File Browser, Finder and Transcript improvements System Refactoring command migration and registry Scoped extensions and selector semantics Clean blocks and debugger/evaluation behavior ClassBuilder, trait and superclass correctness Compiler API split and method installation UnifiedFFI value holders, FFIMethod , callbacks and bootstrap resets Command-line debugger Debugger / client-model cleanup Package/baseline modularization and bootstrap dependency cleanup Morphic / UIManager dependency reduction FastTable, text, graphics, Zinc and Zodiac fixes Sindarin script tooling Code editor / code presenter work List, tree and filtering behavior Dialog, window and modal behavior Action/command enhancements and cleanup Morphic backend and layout fixes Virtual machine Frame unification and stack management improvements, delivering substantial interpreter and execution engine cleanups RISC-V JIT support, expanding platform coverage and future-proofing VM development New memory management capabilities, including direct old-space allocation and numerous GC and allocation improvements Extensive compiler and Slang/C translation work, with many correctness fixes, new tests, and improved inspection tools Platform and build modernization, including SDL updates, improved CI, cross-build support, and updated third-party dependencies Large-scale cleanup and refactoring efforts across the VM, interpreter, Cogit, PICs, and infrastructure Development Effort This new version is the result of 978 Pull Requests integrated just in the Pharo repository. We have closed 616 issues since Pharo 13. The project now counts 432 forks and 1,494 stars on GitHub. We also have a lot of work in the separate projects that are included in each Pharo release: https://github.com/pharo-spec/NewTools https://github.com/pharo-spec/Spec https://github.com/pharo-vcs/Iceberg https://github.com/pharo-graphics/Roassal https://github.com/pillar-markup/Microdown https://github.com/pillar-markup/BeautifulComments https://github.com/pharo-project/pharo-vm Contributors We always say Pharo is yours. It is yours because we made it for you, but most importantly, because it is made by the invaluable contributions of our great community (yourself). A large community of people from all around the world contributed to Pharo 14 by making pull requests, reporting bugs, participating in discussion threads, providing feedback, and a lot of helpful tasks in all our community channels. Thank you all for your contributions. The Pharo Team Discover Pharo: https://pharo.org/features Try Pharo: http://pharo.org/download Learn Pharo: http://pharo.org/documentation 26 October 2026 <-- What people do with Pharo Pharo is developed by an international community of open-source developers, coordinated and maintained by the pharo consortium and receives essential support from Inria, RMOD, CNRS, UDL, Cristal and many others.
